ST. PATRICK'S DAY CELEBRATION ON SATURDAY NEXT    REFERENCE TO MEMBER FOR FORT WILLIAM
speechtext:
On a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say that for many years past the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) and I have made representations annually to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and the late prime minister, Mr. W. L. Mackenzie King, for the adjournment of the house so that Irishmen and their friends might properly celebrate St. Patrick's day. This year the seventeenth of March falls on a Saturday, so that it will not be necessary to make that request; it is coming automatically. We, with the hon. member for Saskatoon city (Mr. Knight), invite all Irishmen and their friends to celebrate as they should because Saturday is followed by Sunday, and Sunday will be the day for recuperation.
I have one other request to make on behalf of, perhaps, the Irish. We have had with us for the past fifteen or sixteen years the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor). Recently he celebrated his seventy-eighth birthday. He was applauded, I believe, by members on all sides of the house. He is not only my friend but is a friend of all of us. Having given the very best of services during the week to humanity in this house, he has also gone out on Sunday and looked after the spiritual welfare of many sections of this country. The other day on looking over a list of the members of the other place and their occupations, I found that there was not one clergyman among them. I am now suggesting that, inasmuch as we have several clergymen around this corner of the house who can also minister to the needs of the other sections of it, it would be a splendid gesture on the part of the Prime Minister to allow the hon. member for Fort William to go to the other place so that he may look after the members there.

speechtext: The house resumed, from Thursday, March 15, consideration of the motion of Mr. Howe for the second reading of Bill No. 5, to amend the Canadian Wheat Board Act, 1935, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Ross (Souris).

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: PROVISION FOR EARLY DISTRIBUTION OF PAYMENTS AT END OF POOL PERIOD, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in continuing the
remarks that I was making last night on the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross), I wish to come back to what is now under consideration by hon. members. The amendment that has been moved is as follows:
That this bill be not now read a second time but that further consideration thereof be deferred until this house has had an opportunity to record its opinion on the government's announced decision with respect to the final settlement of the five-year wheat pool and on the government's mishandling of the sale of wheat and other grains covered by the Canadian Wheat Board Act.

Different members on the opposite side have taken exception to the word "mishandling." Several members on the other side of the house have emphasized that it is the use of the word "mishandling" which makes it impossible for them to consider this amendment. May I suggest to them, and to others who have not expressed themselves but who may have been directing their attention to this particular word, that they consider the grounds upon which the government has announced that it proposes to make a payment of $65 million.
We have the unqualified statement of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), supported by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), that nothing is owing by the British government under the wheat contract. I would remind hon. members that this statement by the Minister of Trade and Commerce is borne out in full and very emphatically by the papers tabled in this house last night.
These records of the minutes of a meeting held in London last May and the subsequent confirmation of the position taken by the government of Great Britain make it abundantly clear that the statement made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce on June 5 of last year in this house, in very brief form, indicating that this government concurred in the position taken by the government of Great Britain, was not only accurate but was an understatement of the extent to which complete and unmistakable agreement had been reached on that point by the two governments.
That being so, no matter on what other ground the money may be owing, it is certainly not owing under the wheat contract. In that respect we must take the position of this government, supported by the records, especially between the two governments, as evidence of that fact. Therefore any money that is being paid is being paid upon some other ground. If it is not on the ground that this government mishandled, and grossly mishandled, the wheat, then on what ground is it? It can only be on the ground that there was such a mishandling of wheat by this government that there is a substantial debt to the farmers of western Canada.
No other proposition has been put forward. It has been mishandled to the extent that some very substantial obligation, in the opinion of this government, was created independently of the contract between the governments of Great Britain and Canada. Therefore the payment that is announced by the government is something that the government now is saying they will do because of the way they let down the farmers of western 80709-85	*
Canadian Wheat Board Act Canada in their handling of wheat. That is precisely the position, and therefore "mishandling" is a very moderate statement in these circumstances which have led to the announcement that the government now makes.
But, Mr. Speaker, we have sought from the government some evidence of the way in which they arrived at a figure of this kind. It is true that at this stage the house is not called upon to vote for or against this payment. It is appropriate at the present stage, however, that the house should know the way in which the government arrived at this figure, in view of the fact that the government itself has chosen this debate as the time to make their statement in regard to the subject.
The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has added nothing yet to the information already before the house as to the way in which the figure of $65 million emerged. Let us reduce it to a simple form. The Prime Minister said: "No; it is perfectly true there was no obligation on the part of the government of the United Kingdom. Nevertheless, after the succession of events which had occupied our thoughts for some time last summer, we did become aware of the fact that there was discontent among the farmers of western Canada. We thought it advisable therefore, when we learned that the Prime Minister of Great Britain was going to be here in December that we should indicate to him that there was this discontent; and that although all obligations under the contract had been disposed of, nevertheless they might take into consideration the wisdom or otherwise of recognizing that discontent, and presumably giving that discontent some measurable terms in money."
The Prime Minister has explained that the Prime Minister of Great Britain obviously was not impressed with the obligation on the British government to deal with the problem of discontent in Canada. Nevertheless he sought the consent of the Prime Minister of Great Britain to speak to the Chancellor of the Exchequer on this subject. Having received the assurance that there would be no discourtesy implied in that procedure, he carried forward his intention and evidently received the same reply there.
The information which he communicated to the government upon his return evidently did not close this subject completely, because the Minister of Agriculture then decided to carry the matter further, and go to Great Britain to discuss the subject. The Minister of Agriculture, however, did not base this upon discontent; he based his claim upon an

Canadian Wheat Board Act obligation which he alleged existed, and he left the impression in the house that that obligation had been unfulfilled.

We know that an attempt was made, no matter how skilfully the proposal was cloaked in diplomatic terms,

to have the government of the United Kingdom take up the balance of the loan of $65 million so that it would appear to be paying the government of Canada the remainder of the obligations under the wheat contract. But the government of the United Kingdom refused to have any part in an improper subterfuge of that kind which would have misled the people of Canada as to what was actually taking place. It is in the light of the attempt that was made-and that attempt incidentally is the only basis for the figure we now have before us with regard to the payment of an obligation which this government believes it owes the farmers of western Canada-that we must examine the minutes of the meeting of May 22 last. speechtext:
The exhibition we have seen this afternoon of evasion of a reasonable explanation by ministers of the crown is simply another demonstration of the contempt in which parliament is held by members of the government which is about to ask this house to support a payment to the farmers of western Canada for the government's mishandling of the wheat purchases from those farmers during the past four years.
When members of this house find these evasions and these devices for avoiding responsibility so humorous it is about time that they came face to face with their own responsibilities as members, because they are responsible along with the government if they fail to express any desire for that information which would make it possible for the members of this house to pass judgment upon facts with some knowledge of what those facts really are.
Hon. members may find it very easy to impress themselves by their laughter and desk thumping, but that is confined to this chamber. Honour, public decency, respect for the hard-won traditions of a free parliament will never be determined by a vote in this or any other legislative chamber. Those are matters that are determined on other grounds. Unless the government repudiates the minister who has been guilty of this shameful and shameless conduct, then it must itself accept responsibility for recklessly endangering mutual confidence between the governments of Canada and Great Britain, which is so vitally important to us and to the whole free world at this time. Do not let anyone say that this is not being endangered. I have read from Hansard statements already made in this house reflecting on the government of a sister nation within the commonwealth. You have heard remarks of hon. members in the house this afternoon indicating that they share the same opinion. A minister of the crown, knowing what was done last May to confirm the final settlement of the wheat contract, has sought rMr. Drew.]
to convey the impression that the British government fell down on its obligations, that it did not play ball with this country, to use the expression of one hon. member. The last thing that should be countenanced in these critical days is an attempt by any member of this or any other government in Canada to try to save his political hide at the expense of the good will between two of the most important nations in the commonwealth.

Canadian Wheat Board Act products, it would cost the average income tax payer of Canada $250. When these items come before us like this, I must say that I find myself in one hundtred per cent agreement with what the leader of the opposition stated this afternoon, namely, that you cannot laugh these things off. When we have people in every walk of life today struggling with the high cost of living, struggling to keep their sons and daughters at university, struggling to meet their budgets, men and women in all walks of life, then losses that mean $250 apiece to every income tax payer are matters that should not be laughed off, no matter how big the support you have in this parliament.
I am not trying to make insinuations. I know that there are those who think there must be a polecat under the table with regard to this agreement. Because some group expected it, and because we all expect a provincial election, should we make a settlement so arbitrarily made as this one?
I claim, Mr. Speaker, that the minister owes to this house an explanation as to what the general policy is going to be. All those agreements I have mentioned, all the agreements we had with Britain for foodstuffs, have gone by the board. We have one for five years with the world, in the international wheat agreement. If this government refuse to take the advice or council of the wheat pools and the western farmers in Canada, and ignore the wheat board, they may make as big a failure of this as they have of the other agreements. Somebody says there is a moral obligation on Britain. Canadian Wheat Board Act Minister saying that where there is no legal obligation). In the time that I have been in parliament, Mr. Speaker, I have never seen an exhibition before similar to the one that we have had since Thursday of last week. We saw the the spectacle of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) rising in his place, and in spite of his full knowledge that the Canadian government had agreed back on May 30 of last year that Britain had fulfilled the wheat agreement in every way, attempt to mislead this house by making statements which have since been proven absolutely false.

In rising to support the amendments to this act, I want first to say how pleased I was when this act was put on the statute books away back in 1935. It was something for which the western farmer had fought a long time. While we can sit back now and criticize the things that the government has done with the board, there is no doubt that the wheat board has given to the grain farmer stability which he never had before. At one time we had in operation two systems which were available to the producer; that is, he could sell his wheat on the open market or he could sell it to the wheat board. But it was found that when wheat was scarce and commanded a good price, the farmers had a tendency to take the big price as long as it lasted and then, when the price fell, they immediately sold their wheat to the board.
It has been a great step forward in western Canada to have the wheat board handle not only wheat but also oats and barley. As to oats and barley, I believe further improvement can be made. But we still have speculation in rye and flax. You cannot go to a farmers' meeting in western Canada without being confronted with the questions: When is the wheat board going to take over rye and flax? When are they also going to be taken off the speculative market? Why should the farmer have to sell his flax and rye on a speculative market when we have the facilities for handling those grains in a pooling system?
I should like to quote from the Toronto Daily Star of January 29, 1951. This statement relates to some remarks the editor made with reference to a statement made by Professor McDougall of Queen's university, and is as follows:
The strong feelings expressed by the farm representatives are rooted in the history of Canadian grain marketing. During the many years when grain was traded on the Winnipeg grain exchange, many farmers believed, correctly or incorrectly, that speculators were depriving them of profits. The great majority appear content to have the government market their grain through the Canadian wheat board, with the year's price assured when planting begins. Practical experience, not merely theories or suspicions about private grain companies, underlies prevailing prairie opinion about the wheat pools. These giant co-operatives now handle virtually half the grain produced in the three prairie provinces. Through them the member farmer can assure himself of fair grades on his grain and minimum handling charges. The pools pay the farmers dividends based on the volume of grain they market, and during the quarter-century in which the pools have operated these patronage dividends have totalled more than $27 million. To stay in business, some private grain companies have been forced to do likewise. Where else in Canada do private firms pay dividends to their customers?
In view of such results, it is futile to tell grain growers that their pools have no real value.

This shows what the farmer thinks. We have come a long way since the days of Roderick McKenzie, Colin Burnell, Dan Chapman and other men like that who fought for the right to be allowed to load their own grain in a car without putting it through the elevator. Along with these can be added names of men from Saskatchewan and Alberta who have been pioneers in the farm movement in those provinces. The dreams of these men are gradually becoming true, but as long as we leave rye and flax in a speculative market we still have something to fight for.
Last fall it was estimated that western Canada would have a crop of flax of about three million bushels; that is, for the 1950-51 crop year. Statistics show that about two and a half million bushels were delivered up to about December 1, so the tremendous increase that took place in flax prices never gave any benefit to the man who produced the flax; because I would say 75 per cent of the farmers market their crops when they have to make their payments-and that is in the fall-and do not wait until the spring to sell their crops. Of course some farmers do; some who are financially well fixed can play the market, and delight in doing so. But the bona fide farmer who is out for stability and steady prices over a period of years does not try to play the market.
I should like to draw to the attention of hon. members the fluctuation that took place in flax in six months. On August 1, 1950, the price of No. 1 C. W. flax was $3.63; on September 1, 1950, it was $3.82; on October 2, 1950, it was $3.68; on November 1, 1950, it was $3.58R on December 1, 1950, it was $3.81; on January 2, 1951, it was $4.21; and on February 1, 1951, it was $5.71. You have a spread there of $2.08. The farmer did not get that. That went into other channels. I leave you to guess who got it.
Under the pooling system all producers agree to accept the same price, which would in most cases be an average price. I would at this time urge the government to place flax and rye under the wheat board because I honestly believe it is beneficial to the producers of grain, no matter what grain he is producing. I am not going to deal with the speculation which has taken place on rye over a number of years, as I have put that story on record here before. But what has happened to flax and rye on a speculative market could happen to any grain, and we know that the wheat board could and can protect the farmer.
The wheat board is still using the speculative market to sell oats and barley against the wishes of a large majority of the western
Canadian Wheat Board Act producers. This is borne out by some of the recent pool conventions where resolutions were passed asking that the wheat board discontinue the use of the speculative market in the selling of oats and barley. The Canadian Federation of Agriculture in their most recent brief asked that the use of the speculative market be reduced or eliminated altogether.
I would have liked to bring in an amendment at this time to include these things, but I have read very carefully the remarks you made two days ago, Mr. Speaker, and I had an idea you would rule me out of order. I want to play safe, but to my way of thinking as a layman, rye and flax are tied in with barley, oats and wheat. The amendment that I would have liked to bring in at this time would have been quite all right so far as I am concerned, but I have never been able to look at a thing in a legal way as you can, sir, and sometimes when I hear some of the legal opinions expressed in this house I am glad that my mind does not act in that way.
I think I have made my point quite clear. I do hope the day is not far distant when the western farmer will market all his grain through the pooling system, and through the wheat board. While I shake my head and frown sometimes when I see and hear the things that the wheat board is blamed for in connection with political manoeuvring, I hope that not only this government but any other government that is in power in Canada will get rid of that sort of thing and not make the wheat board a political tool.

I should like
to say a few words in support of what the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bryce) has just said. We are supporting the amendments which are in this Bill No. 5, which is now before the house, but I wonder whether they will be implemented or not, because last year we passed an amendment in this house to the wheat board act, which gave the government authority to add two additional members to the wheat board. So far as I know that has not been implemented up to date.
In my opinion the present members of the wheat board are overworked. As a matter of fact, we are simply killing these men. They are valuable men; they are men who have done a very good job for the western farmer in the marketing of his grain. Probably they are three of the best informed men in grain marketing in the world today. It is a shame that we should overwork them. It is a shame that they should not have some more assistance on the board, because the marketing of coarse grain has become quite a problem.

Canadian Wheat Board Act
Some of the things that we are suggesting, and I am going to suggest as we go along in this debate, are not offered as a criticism of the wheat board itself but as a criticism of the authority the government is giving them in the matter of the marketing of our grain. I am sure that when the western farmers asked that their grain be marketed through the board they had three major objectives in mind. First, they preferred an average price for the grain that they had to sell over the years. They have tried for the last thirty or forty years to guess the market as to when they could get the best price for their grain, and they have come to the conclusion that as far as they were concerned they would rather see their grain sold by some organization or some board and obtain an average price for that grain over the years so that they would not have to guess the market. The second reason why they preferred to have their grain marketed under a board system was to get away from the speculative market and to prevent speculation in their products.
The third reason-and I want the eastern people to remember this-was that we in western Canada wanted to get our grain to the ultimate consumer in the most direct method that was possible and with the least margin between what the consumers in eastern Canada had to pay and what we as western producers received.
Under the present wheat board system I think we have gone only part of the way in accomplishing those objectives. The first objective we have accomplished fully. That is, we do get the average price that is obtained for our grain over the years, and we do not have to guess the market.
The second matter, that of preventing speculation, has only been partially accomplished because the board are continuing to use the Winnipeg grain exchange in the marketing of our coarse grains. It has been very definitely indicated to the government by various farm organizations that they would prefer to have the board stop using the Winnipeg grain exchange as the method of marketing of coarse grains.
I hold in my hand the twenty-sixth annual report of -the Saskatchewan Co-operative Producers, Limited, and under the heading "coarse grains marketing" the following appears:
A resolution passed at the last annual meeting of delegates urged that the speculative element in marketing grain should- be eliminated and a marketing system established which would ensure stability in prices, both for producer and consumer. The resolution also asked that the wheat board's coarse grains marketing policy be changed to give effect to the wishes of organized farmers in this connection. This matter was also taken up with the govem-

ment in the submission above referred to and it was urged that the marketing of coarse grains should be the responsibility solely of the Canadian wheat board and that the speculative market should be closed.
The Canadian Federation of Agriculture in their last submission to the cabinet, which they presented- just recently, had this to say: Our convention favoured the continuation of the wheat board as the sole marketing agency for coarse grains but they expressed the view that the board should make only the minimum use of the future market in order that experience may point a way to a sounder and more acceptable marketing policy.
In other words, they want the board to discontinue the Winnipeg grain exchange except in a moderate way.
I had a return tabled in the house recently in answer to a question of mine. In the question I asked the government as to the amount of sales of each coarse grain in the Winnipeg grain exchange. The return was tabled on February 9. I am just going to give the round figures. It says that the wheat board bought 80 million bushels of oats from the western producer and 53 million bushels of barley. It shows that of that 80 million bushels of oats which they had bought from the western producer, 65,785,000 bushels were sold through the Winnipeg grain exchange. Of the 53 million bushels of barley bought from the western farmer,
37,808,000	bushels were disposed of on the speculative market, through the Winnipeg grain exchange. I know that with the board controlling all this grain there is not the same speculative element on the market that there was before we had the board, but nevertheless there is -a speculative market, and I want to give the reason why. The reason is this:	-climatic conditions in this
country are such that when we thresh our crop in western Canada in August, September and October there are large deliveries of coarse grains. Those coarse grains must be moved or can be moved more cheaply to eastern Canada before navigation closes.
As it now operates, the wheat board does not ship grain, -except to Port Arthur and Fort William. Therefore they have to sell large quantities of that grain, as is indicated in- the return made to me, on the speculative market in- Winnipeg. They have to sell it on the Winnipeg grain exchange, so that the commission firms may get possession of the grain and move it to eastern Canada before navigation closes.
The return tabled- in my name shows that sales of oats by the Canadian wheat board in the months of August, September, October and November in the 1949-50 crop year were, in August, 6,843,319 bushels; September, 8,816,078; October, 11,158,399 and November, 11,653,206. The other months dropped to 5

million or less. During these same months there were sold on the Winnipeg grain exchange the following amounts of oats: August, 6,596,000 bushels; September, 7,365,000; October,
8,880,000	and November, 10,128,000.
This grain was sold to the commission firms through the Winnipeg grain exchange. During those months the price of oats in particular was much lower than it was in the early months of the following year. By March the price had jumped from approximately 90 cents, as it had been in the fall, to well over $1.25.
My contention is that we will never have a satisfactory wheat board until it is prepared to move this grain from western Canada to the terminal elevators in eastern Canada, to keep control of the grain, to establish selling agencies in eastern Canada and to sell the grain direct to the consumers in this part of the country. To do that they will have to have more personnel on the board. But as it stands at the present time, the small consumer or small co-operative in eastern Canada, the small chap in this part of the country who has a feed plant and grinds that feed to sell in his neighbourhood, finds that he cannot deal directly with the board.
I know the provisions state that the board can sell directly to him. Nevertheless the procedure is such that he is not able to buy directly from the board. I have before me a copy of a letter sent to one of the eastern mill owners who is grinding feed to serve his own locality. This man wrote to the board to see if he could buy directly from it, and this was the advice they gave him:
It is the general practice for eastern feeders to procure their supplies of feeding grains through the commercial channels in the Winnipeg grain exchange. Most of these organizations maintain stocks in positions applicable to the requirements of the eastern trade. Daily quotations may be procured from such firms. All the forwarding details and collections are the responsibility of such forwarding firms.
Then, proceeding to tell him how he can buy directly from the board, they say:
The Canadian wheat board does not forward coarse grains beyond the in store Fort William/Port Arthur position. If you so desire, however, this board will sell such grains as they have on hand to eastern customers upon application. The prices will be those established at the close of each day's market. Such prices are in effect from the close of one day until 9.30 the following morning. These prices are available at all large trading centres across Canada, and are published daily by the Canadian wheat board.
When such purchases are made, it is the responsibility of the buyer to appoint an agent such as a bank or an accredited legal firm to take delivery of documents covering the grain required. It is also the responsibility of the purchaser to arrange with terminal elevators at the head of the lakes for the loading of such grain. You will also be required to file orders with tne railroads giving proper
Canadian Wheat Board Act
destination. The Canadian wheat board will deliver to your agent the warehouse receipt covering the grade of grain required in some designated elevator in Fort William/Port Arthur. Such terminal elevator would require that these documents be turned over to them before the grain is loaded out and billed for your account.
And then they go on to say:
The procedure is rather involved and I doubt that any saving would be made by you in following such a course.
The average small co-operative in eastern Canada, in other words, just does not have an agent in Winnipeg. He does not have an agent at the head of the lakes. The result is that he must depend upon a commission firm in Winnipeg to bring that grain forward to eastern Canada and thus make it available. The result was that this year our harvest was late and very little of our grain was moved into forward positions in eastern Canada to serve the eastern feeder during the winter months. I believe if the board had been handling the matter and had not been depending upon commission firms it could have moved greater quantities of that grain into forward positions in eastern Canada.
After all, those of us in western Canada are interested in making our feed grains available to our customers in eastern Canada in the best possible way. We would like to see that grain placed down here in eastern elevators. We want the grades maintained right up to the time the ultimate consumer gets that grain. At the present time the grain loses its identity at the head of the lakes. The commission firm buying it up there brings it to eastern Canada and is permitted to mix it or do anything it likes. The result is that the feeder in eastern Canada is not getting as good a grade as he should be. I have seen many samples of feed grains being sold in eastern Canada, and they certainly have not been the grades of grain we sell in the west. It is mixed before it goes to the small mill owner, the small crushing plant or the co-operative in eastern Canada.
I do not think our wheat board will be the success it should be in the marketing of our coarse grains until it takes the responsibility of bringing the grain forward to eastern Canada and placing it in terminal elevators, so that the producers in eastern Canada may go to those agencies and make direct purchases of their requirements, in the knowledge that they are getting a fair sample of the grain they are supposed to be purchasing. I believe this could be done; to my mind there could be no objection to it.
That is what our farm organizations are seeking. A year ago, because of the quality of the feed being sold in eastern Canada, the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, in their presentation to the cabinet said, as it is set

Canadian Wheat Board Act out at page 12, that an investigation should be made into the marketing and distributing of feed grains going into protein feeds in Canada, because of the mixing which takes place. I believe much of that could be prevented if the wheat board were to move the grain to forward positions in eastern Canada.
Another matter I should like to bring to the attention of the government is that we should make greater use of the port of Churchill. At present there is in storage at that point approximately 450,000 bushels of grain. The capacity of the port is 2,500,000 bushels. It has a drying capacity of from 15,000 to
20,000	bushels of grain every twenty-four hours. We are not moving any grain to that port for drying. I suppose the reason is that the wheat board believes that that grain which needs drying will be difficult to sell to European buyers out of that port when ships are available next July.
I would point out that a lot of this damp and tough grain is feed grain which could be moved into that port, dried, and then moved to the maritime provinces, if the wheat board wanted to take the responsibility of chartering vessels, to the elevators at Saint John and Halifax and made available for feed in eastern Canada. I hope the government will endeavour to make the wheat board the useful agency that it can be in the marketing of our grains.
I agree with the amendments provided for by this bill. As a matter of fact when I spoke on the speech from the throne I indicated that there had not been some mention made of amendments to the wheat board act which would do exactly what is done by section 3 of this bill, that is, give the wheat board authority at the end of each crop year to close out the pool and make some arrangement to take over the grain that remained and carry it forward into the next pool year.
When the bill is in committee we will have some suggestions to make and amendments to offer. I think perhaps the bill is loosely worded because it does not indicate at what price the government shall take over the grain. It simply states that the government may take over the grain. I think there should be an obligation on the government to take it over within a stated period.
We would then be passing a bill which meant something, not just placing another piece of legislation on the statute books as we did with the amendment last year to the wheat board act to increase the membership to five. I hope the government will implement that amendment passed last year so that this board will be able to do an even more efficient job than they have been doing in the past.

I believe they have been doing a most efficient job in the marketing of our grain as far as their end of it is concerned. I do not agree with all the policies that they have had to carry out on behalf of the government but, as I say, they have done an efficient job. I am one hundred per cent behind the board method of handling our grain in western Canada.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright) has referred to the amendment passed last year to increase the board membership to five. I certainly endorse that wholeheartedly and I would like to see one of the new members come either from Ontario or eastern Canada. I know the feed men and dealers in Ontario would strongly support this idea as they feel it would give a more efficient handling of feed in eastern Canada. I strongly support the suggestion.
Motion (Mr. Howe) agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Beaudoin in the chair.
On section 1-"Pool period" defined.

Mr. Chairman, I have had to keep quiet for some days because I have taken full advantage of every opportunity afforded me to speak. However, I am not going to go over all the details that have been dealt with. I was one of the members who had questioned the Minister of Trade and Commerce on March 5 and I was disappointed that I could not speak at that time. Some people may wonder why I have not spoken again, and I am taking advantage of this opportunity to say a few words about coarse grains.
I am sure that our party is in favour generally of these amendments, but I should like to say just a few words about oats. I have always been a supporter of the wheat board, and am still. I am in favour of these amendments in principle, but there has been considerable dissatisfaction in connection with feed grain. As an example, a neighbour of mine has been growing registered seed. His product was being properly inspected and as he lived only twenty miles from the United States boundary there were people from the United States coming over and offering 90 cents a bushel for his oats. He wrote to the wheat board for a permit to sell his oats to the United States buyers who were ready to truck it away, but was refused.
Of course he was.
I think some of the regulations are pretty stiff under the circumstances. Then there is the other matter that was dealt with by the two speakers just

before we went into committee. I refer to the differential between the price paid to the farmer and what is paid for feed in places like Russell and Glengarry counties close to Ottawa. Last year our final settlement for oats in my neighbourhood was approximately 70 cents, but the hon. member for Russell has stated that on April 5 he paid $76 per ton for oats. You can figure that out into the price per bushel and readily see the difference between what the producer gets and what the consumer in eastern Canada had to pay for his feed grain.
I think something should be done to improve the method of handling. Subsidies are being paid by the taxpayers, of which the producers pay their share, and the feeders down here should have been able to buy oats on a pooling basis at a price much closer to what was received by the producer. I should like to see some improvement made in this connection which would benefit both the producer and the feeder.
I do not want to delay this bill because, as I said, I am quite sure that this party is in favour of the amendments. If there has been hardship in connection with this year's crop it is most essential that some provision be made to meet it. I hope that as we take up the bill section by section something can be done to improve it still further.
Will the minister indicate what is the position in connection with implementing the amendment passed last year to increase the membership of the wheat board?

My bon. friend said that the membership of the wheat board is made up of the ablest men to be found in Canada. I am not sure that he did not say in the world. If I could find a fourth ablest man I would be very glad to appoint him -to the board. It is not easy to get men of that calibre. I am not willing to take anything less. I am not willing to take a man who is not up to the calibre of the three men I have on that board. If my hon. friend can name a man who knows as much about marketing wheat as those three I will be very glad to appoint him.

I am afraid I cannot, but I am afraid that one of these three men will be dead inside of another eighteen months unless some assistance is given. I think you have got to take that into consideration. These men cannot carry the load they are carrying indefinitely. In my opinion even a man who did not have all the qualifications of the three men presently on the board would be better than no man at all.
Canadian Wheat Board Act

I would question that. I would want to have the board tell me that the man I proposed to appoint would actually be a help to them rather than otherwise. I know enough about boards to know that a man who is not competent actually slows down the work of competent men rather than speeding it up. Therefore I am very careful about making the fourth appointment, although I have no objection to doing so, and would do so if the board would indicate to me that the appointment of any certain man would speed up their work.

When the minister introduced this bill he referred to the difficulties and delays caused by the situation the country finds itself in with respect to tough and damp grain. I shall read one sentence only. At page 1052 of Hansard for March 8 he said:
I hope it will be possible to find storage for stocks of tough and damp grain remaining on farms, as well as terminal accommodation for the tough and damp stocks still in country elevators, before warm weather sets in.
I am in this position in this debate. There is no wheat in my constituency but we have in Skeena a very good elevator owned by the dominion government with a capacity of
1,250,000	bushels, constructed by one of the world's outstanding engineers, with a drying capacity of some 48,000 bushels per day, depending of course upon the moisture content of the grain. In view of the fact that this government-owned elevator has stood empty for some six years, and the country as I understand it finding itself with an embarrassingly large quantity of tough and damp grain on hand at the present time, my question to the minister is: Have they considered, and if not will they consider, making use of their own elevator for the purpose of taking care of some of this grain?

I shall be very glad to put that question to the board. I see the members sitting in the gallery so I will be able to do that quite soon. I know that with respect to other wheat crops it has not been found feasible for marketing reasons to use the Prince Rupert elevator as an outlet for west coast grain. I have not inquired from them just what the effect of the tough and damp grain situation is but I will do so. I can assure the hon. member that there is no lack of desire on my part to have the Prince Rupert elevator in operation once again.

I believe the suggestion made by the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright) to increase the number of members of the board is a good one. Sometimes these days heart attacks occur very suddenly, and we would then find it necessary to appoint someone. I know that the minister possibly has

Canadian Wheat Board Act someone in mind, and I believe such a man might carry on the duties of a deputy until such time as he had acquired enough experience to carry on as a regular member.

The minister intimated that if he could find a good man he might possibly consider appointing him to the wheat board, and I should like to ask him to give consideration to my previous suggestion as to the appointment of a member from eastern Canada.

The duty of the board is to market wheat, oats, and barley from the designated area. Eastern Canada is not in the designated area. I think my hon. friend has in mind appointing a man whose objective would not be the same as the objective of the present three members of the wheat board, which is to sell wheat, oats and barley from the western provinces at the best price obtainable.

Last fall, as all members are aware, we had the greatest difficulty getting sufficient cars and elevator space to market even the eight bushel quota which was first established. My question has to do with the quota system. I am in favour of the quota system, and when it is applied equitably I think it is to the advantage of all producers. I should like to know why the eight bushel quota was lifted at a number of points, to my personal knowledge, long before the producers at those points had anywhere near the eight bushels delivered to the elevators. There is one elevator point within a few miles of my home, and I know that on October 5, the Thursday before Thanksgiving, the quota there was lifted entirely. At that time the farmers had marketed only a small portion of the eight bushel quota, and it left marketing at that point in a mess. I know that up until a month or two ago a good many producers in that area had not marketed a bushel of grain. I want to say I am in favour of the quota system but I wonder why consideration was not given to the marketing situation at some of these points before the quota was lifted entirely.

I am afraid I cannot answer that question. The quota system is operated by the wheat board, and I presume it is operated according to their best judgment of how to best take care of the crops in the area. I have heard other suggestions that quotas have been lifted too soon, and while quotas were in effect I have heard suggestions of great injustices that were caused owing to the fact that, while a man could not deliver within the quota of his own elevator, he could deliver into someone else's area. We get complaints both ways. However, I think the

board has had a good deal of experience in operating the quota system, and I am sure they use the best judgment that they can bring to bear on the manner in which the quotas operate.

Could the minister give me a more complete answer on the estimates? On the other hand, if the wheat board report is to be referred to the standing committee on agriculture that will be fine. We will get the information there.
Since my hon. friend has asked about a particular point, a question on the order paper would be referred to the board and would probably elicit the answer he wants.
A month or so ago I referred to the situation that prevailed at Moose Jaw last year. I wonder whether the minister knows anything about that. If he does not, I will leave it to some later date.
I am sorry, I do not know anything about it.

I know that any member of the agricultural committee has the right to call for a meeting thereof, but is the minister prepared to have the wheat board report referred to that committee again? I should like to see that done. I think it is in the interest of the wheat board system to have the board officials appear before the committee. They have always given an excellent account of themselves in the past, and I believe they will do so again. I think the producers of western Canada feel better if the officials of the board appear before the agricultural committee at which time we can go over their annual report.

All I can say at the moment is that consideration will be given to that request. I might remind the hon. member that the overworked wheat board of three members is pretty busy, and it means a week or so away from their normal occupation. However, I will discuss it with the board and give my hon. friend an answer later.

Section agreed to.
Section 2 agreed to.
On section 3-Transfer of wheat from one pool period to subsequent pool period.

Section 3 reads as follows:
The governor in council may authorize the board to adjust its accounts at any time by transferring to the then current pool period all wheat delivered during the preceding pool period and then remaining unsold, and the board shall credit to the accounts for that preceding pool period, and charge against the accounts for the current pool period, such amount as the governor in council deems to be a reasonable price for the wheat so transferred . . .

I think this section gives the governor in council a discretion which it might not be too happy to have. It would have to decide the time at which the transaction should take place. It would have to decide the price at which it would take place; and, whether or not there should be a transaction at all. It seems to me the producers themselves would be much happier if at the end of any one year pool it was mandatory that the transfer of the surplus remaining should be made. My suggestion would be within sixty days after July 31, at the end of any one year pool. I think that will have to be done in any case if the payments are to go out, as they should, shortly after the end of each one year pool period. I do not think our experience in relation to the "have regard to" clause has been too happy. I am not going back to it now, but it was loosely worded and left everyone a great deal of discretion. I do not think the experience of anyone with it was too happy. I am just wondering if the Minister of Trade and Commerce might accept an amendment such as I am going to move, seconded by the hon. member for Melfort:
That clause 3 be amended by deleting therefrom the words "the governor in council may authorize the board to adjust its accounts at any time" and by substituting therefor the following words:	"The
board shall, not later than the 30th day of September in each year, adjust its accounts."
I think that should cover it. After each one year pool period the inventory would be sold to the following one year pool, so the payments could be made say not later than January 1 of the year following the conclusion of the crop year.

I am sorry the government could not accept that amendment. Conditions might be such that the risk would be too great for the second pool to accept. My hon. friend realizes that the transfer of the accounts to the second pool means that the first pool is paid the value of that wheat by the second pool. If we had some accurate way of fixing the value of the wheat at that time, this amendment would be proper, and very often I think it will be possible to safely make the transfer by the date mentioned. This year, however, about half the crop oi a little more was feed grades of wheat. Whether that amount of feed grain would be reduced to manageable proportions by the end of September no one could be sure. If there should be a great quantity of feed wheat to be sold I do not think anyone would care to take the responsibility of putting a price on it and closing out the first pool, leaving the second pool to take all the risks of selling that wheat in the period of the second pool.
Canadian Wheat Board Act
The purpose of this amendment is to permit small lots of wheat to be cleaned up. I have in mind lots of wheat that really could not very much affect the payment of either pool. For instance, you might have a hundred bushels of No. 3 durum wheat left over, which is a difficult grain to sell. Nevertheless that grain must be sold under the present legislation before the pool can be closed out. In the five year pool substantially all the wheat had been sold by the end of September, but there were dribs and drabs left over that were not sold until well into December. Therefore the final payment on that five year pool was delayed several months for no particular financial reason.

This amendment would permit the governor in council to set the price of wheat for the carry-over and they could take into account any conditions that had prevailed during the preceding year in relation to feed wheat or anything else. The minister's explanation shows, I think, that this amendment really does not mean very much, if it is only to allow the board to clean up a few hundred bushels of durum wheat or other almost negligible quantities in order to make the final settlement. We shall continue in future to be in the position we sometimes have been in the past, with the farmer not knowing when or on what basis a final settlement will be made. I thought this amendment was intended to take care of this huge quantity of frozen wheat the board now has on hand. If it is not intended to handle a hundred million bushels of wheat, or any quantity of that nature, then the wheat board may have a carry-over of this frozen wheat for two years or even longer. Certainly the western producers will not be satisfied to have the final payment on this year's crop dangling before them for another year or another two years or another four years, with the governor in council having discretion to turn it into another pool period and play around with the wheat in that respect. If the minister cannot accept our amendment I am afraid that will be the end of it, but certainly the explanation by the minister will not meet the objections of the western producers against the final settlement of any one year pool being extended for a long period of time after that pool comes to an end.

Mr. Speaker, I am not going to detain the house long in connection with this bill, but I wish to say a few words in support of it because of its great importance to the people and to the economy of British Columbia.
All members of this house and, I think, most people in the country realize that the party to which I belong favours public ownership of transportation, communications, and things of this type particularly. When the bill was under discussion on Tuesday, March 6, the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright) dealt at some length with our policy in that connection and moved the following amendment:
That this bill be not now read a second time but that further consideration thereof be deferred until this house has had an opportunity to record its opinion that consideration should be given to the construction and operation of pipe lines by a crown corporation, or by a public agency owned and controlled by the government of Canada.

I am sorry, Mr. Speaker,
if I am out of order; but I just wanted to mention the fact in order to re-emphasize our position in this connection. The motion was lost by a vote of 172 to 12, so we in this party realize that at this time there is not among the members of this house support for the principle of public ownership with respect to oil or gas pipe lines. Realizing that fact, Mr. Speaker, we are supporting the principle of the bill because we believe that the building of this oil pipe line will be of great advantage to the people of British Columbia, to the economy of British Columbia and to Canada as a whole.
Before proceeding with my brief remarks, Mr. Speaker, I want to congratulate the sponsor of this bill, the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Laing), on the detailed information he gave the house on the motion for second reading of this bill. I have sat in this house and heard bills of this type introduced on second reading, when the sponsors gave an extremely sketchy account of the purpose and the intentions of the bill. I am of the opinion that the attitude of some members, such as the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank) and the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Gibson), in requiring fuller explanation, has caused members introducing pipe line bills to realize that hon. members are not going to be satisfied with just a sketchy introduction. I forgot to mention the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton), but I include him at this time and also the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Sinclair).

I must say that we appreciated the information given to the house on the motion for second reading. The hon. member for Vancouver South told us the exact location of the route-that has not happened on another occasion-namely, from Edmonton to Vancouver through the Yellow-head pass. He gave us information as to the capacity of the pipe. He gave us the history and record of the company. He gave us information as to the use of Canadian

personnel in construction and in maintenance, and as to the use of Canadian materials. He gave us information as to the potential markets. He also gave us a great deal of other useful information which we have had the opportunity to reread before this bill came before us for debate again this evening. We appreciate this procedure, and we hope it is a practice which will be followed by other members introducing bills of this type.
I was pleased indeed, Mr. Speaker, to note that the hon. member stressed the fact that this was an all-Canadian route. After my recollections of the debate on pipe lines last year, I am pleased indeed to see the hon. member for Vancouver South standing shoulder to shoulder in this house with that delightful, irrepressible and indefatigable gentleman, the hon. member for Fraser Valley, to fight for an all-Canadian route for gas pipe lines and for oil pipe lines. I think the house and the country owe the hon. member for Fraser Valley particularly a debt of gratitude for focusing public attention, in his own unique and, shall I say, inimitable manner, on a matter of great importance. I trust that when this oil pipe line is constructed from Edmonton to Vancouver, a gas pump will be erected in Chilliwack to commemorate his efforts in this respect.
We are delighted to know that this is the second bill that has come before the house this session in which the sponsor says the main line of the gas or oil concern will follow an all-Canadian route; because that means a great deal to British Columbia in this case and to Canada in general. It means the use of Canadian resources by Canadians first. It means the use of Canadian materials in construction and in maintenance. It means employment for Canadians. It means permanent tax revenue for the provincial government and for the federal government. The construction of this oil pipe line will mean a great deal to the further development of British Columbia and that development will be to the general advantage of Canada. I hope that the bill passes this evening and goes to a committee so that we can hear the rest of what appears to us to be a most interesting story in connection with the further development of our great province, British Columbia.

Mr. Speaker, in the months that we have listened to these pipe line bills, I have more or less viewed the operations with a jaundiced eye because I thought that not only were politics involved but that a great deal of money was behind the people who were seeking incorporation. I did not view with much favour at the last session the efforts of some people
16,	1951
Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line to tell us that an all-Canadian route could be constructed. I want to tell the house tonight that I have now found that I am wrong. I am wrong for one reason. I am still not convinced that it will be financially successful for the pipe line to be built through the Yellowhead route; but after listening to the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Laing) the other night I came to the conclusion that he had a good story to tell, and I congratulate him on telling that story. Not only that, but there is some confirmation of the introduction that he gave to this bill.
Since he talked in the house the British American Oil Company have decided to build a $10 million oil refinery in my constituency of Burnaby. That means a tremendous amount to me and to the people of my riding. We are not an industrial riding; we are a dormitory municipality. W depend on the city of Vancouver for most of our pay cheques. Here is an opportunity that I have to get behind something that is really good for my people, and after listening to the hon. member for Vancouver South the other night I will tell you now, sir, that I intend to support this bill with all the endeavour that I can put at my command.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and referred to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines.
The house resumed, from Friday, March 9, consideration of the motion of Mr. Apple-whaite for the second reading of Bill No. 116, respecting British Columbia Telephone Company.

As
usual, Mr. Speaker, I am to be assisted in a minor way by a lesser light from my own province.
That will hold him.

Because of what happened tonight, Mr. Speaker, in connection with another bill, I would suggest through you to hon. members that they come earlier on Tuesday night to get a good seat to hear the excellent reason why the preceding bill received the excellent reception it did. I have myself prepared one or two things to say on that occasion, and I assure you that there will be other hon. members from he province of British Columbia who will endeavour to gain converts, as we have done in the past year.
I said the other night, Mr. Speaker, in connection with this bill, that I am in favour of the increased capital asked for by the company but not to the extent called for in the bill. One reason why I am not in favour

British Columbia Telephone Company of the increase asked for is that some years ago when this company applied for an increase we asked for certain information. I well remember the hon. member for Van-couver-Quadra (Mr. Green) who was then the hon. member for Vancouver South asking for and receiving the dear guarantee from the telephone company that no increase in rates would be asked for because of the increase in capitalization. We have now found that that was not true. Two increases have been asked for within one year by the telephone company and have been granted by the board of transport commissioners. No doubt other speakers from the city of Vancouver will go into detail and give some of the reasons why that city does not think the capital should be increased to the extent asked for by the sponsor.
I am not from the city of Vancouver, but my district is particularly interested in the lack of service, poor service and lack of additional telephone connections that exist. We dispute definitely the statement made, I believe by the sponsor, although I am not sure of that, but certainly by the representatives of the company, that it has not been able to improve the service or extend it because of the lack of capital. In other words, the reason they are asking for this immense increase is to increase their services, give better connections and better service.
In order that that argument may be answered right now let me point out to you that at the time they put in their application they had the privilege of increasing their capital by $5 million under the last increase they asked for here. They still had $5 million left. The city of Vancouver has gone to a great deal of trouble in this connection. Naturally they should. They represent by far the largest portion of the population of the province of British Columbia.
If you remember, sir, I mentioned the other night that this is one of the finest companies we have. They have an excellent management. If that management were allowed to manage the affairs of the company I do not believe that we would have the poor service we now have nor would they require the immense increase in capital that is being asked for. If these Canadians in Vancouver were allowed to manage the company none of these things would be necessary, but the most amazing thing, Mr. Speaker, is that the management in Vancouver cannot run their company. I want to qualify that to this extent. I believe they are still allowed to hire a janitor or fire a gardener on some of the lawns in front of their offices without consulting their parent company in Montreal. If they want to hire somebody higher up
[Mr. Cruickshank.i

than the janitor apparently they would have to consult the parent company in Montreal.
They have a licence contract, Mr. Speaker, which provides for an annual payment by the B.C. Telephone Company of 1 per cent of its gross operating revenues to the parent company, the Anglo-Canadian Telephone Company of Montreal. This Montreal company is a holding company and through its ownership of common stock controls the following companies operating in British Columbia: British Columbia Telephone Company; Canadian (B.C.) Telephone and Supplies Limited; Dominion Directory Company Limited; Chilliwack Telephones Limited; Kootenay Telephone Company, Limited; Mission Telephone Company Limited and NorthWest Telephone Company.
Probably one reason why I am particularly interested in these companies is that the Chilliwack Telephones Limited and the Mission Telephone Company Limited happened to go through the finest riding of Canada.
Where is that?

My colleague who sits to my left, the junior member from Coast-Capilano, says "louder". I would presume that he would get up, in due course and, without the aid of the new microphones we are to have in the chamber, would succeed in making his voice heard in every corner of the chamber in defence of the rights of his province, and on behalf of the people in his riding who unfortunately have to pay exorbitant rates for their telephone service. If my voice does not carry to the far corners of the chamber, we will hear from that great exponent, no doubt, that the service is needed for the people of Vancouver. I have no doubt the hon. member for Coast-Capi-lano, assisted by his colleagues from greater Vancouver, will endeavour to prove, as I am attempting to do, that this capital should not be increased to the exorbitant amount of $75 million. Perhaps that is wishful thinking. However perhaps some of my junior colleagues will do as they did eventually last year in connection with another matter which affected British Columbia; perhaps they will get on the bandwagon.
I do not want to take up too much time of the house. I am making no attempt to stage a filibuster on this telephone bill; I hope it goes through tonight. However I would feel derelict in my duty to the people I represent if I failed to object to this request for what I consider to be an excessive increase in capitalization.

I said the other night, and I now repeat, that 1 believe they should have some increase in capital, but not to the extent of $50 million -and I am using their own figures. The sum I would hope might find favour-and I am not going to move an amendment at this time; I shall do so in committee-would be an extension by $20 million. This would be in addition to the $5 million they now have available. My reason for not moving at this time is exactly that indicated by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Gibson) who in connection with another matter this afternoon said he was not sure he had a seconder. I notice that my seconder, the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll), is not in his seat at the moment-and I am not sure that any of my colleagues from British Columbia would second it. They might want $50 million.
The figures given by the experts from the city of Vancouver would permit an expenditure of $10 million a year, and thus enable the company to carry on for from six to ten years, through an increase in their capitalization of $20 million. At the end of that time they couldi come back to the house and ask for more.
Unlike the Bell Telephone Company and other telephone companies in Canada, the B.C. Telephone Company must appear before the board of transport commissioners in the matter of rates. Our public utilities commissioner has no control in the matter. The only weapon the people of British Columbia have, in so far as rates are concerned, is through the jurisdiction of the board of transport commissioners. I believe, and I know the people of my riding believe-and I have every reason to think that the people of Vancouver hold the same view, if one may judge by the very excellent brief prepared by experts- that this company could come back in eight or ten years to the board of transport commissioners and ask for a further increase, if at that time it is justified, and I presume it would1 be.
The only thing that would bother them at all-and it should not bather them too much -would be this expenditure of a few thousand dollars. I can show that they have paid $181,000 to one company and $3,000 to another company to get the information. The fact that they have to pay another firm of Vancouver lawyers a few thousand dollars to prepare another brief would not bother them too much in eight or ten years time. As a matter of fact, I am very fond of the lawyer in Vancouver who now represents the company, and I would hope that in eight or ten years from now he may get another fee.
