speechtext: Do you mean there are none there?

I am not worried about that And I can tell my hon. friend, too, that in the Fraser valley exchange we have the best looking girls in the telephone service to be found in any telephone exchange in Canada-and that includes Montreal, too.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The voice of experience.
Have you been all around?

I have not been all around, but I have covered as much territory as I could. I know of course that my hon. friends are trying to get me into shape so that I may speak again on Tuesday night- and, by the way, be here early next Tuesday night if you want to get a seat.
And, on top of that, keep in mind that, as an amateur from a country district, I in company with the then hon. member for Vancouver South-now the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green)-and the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) fought this battle on two former occasions. I would ask hon. members to check through Hansard to find the support we got from the lower mainland or, in fact, from any other quarters, in trying to maintain and regulate telephone rates in British Columbia.
Of course hon. members from greater Vancouver have before them exactly the same brief that I have, prepared by experts. I am sure that with their immense ability, their superior knowledge, their super-desire to serve the people of their districts and of the province, when I take my seat they will be clamouring to speak. I can visualize, Mr. Speaker, the difficulty you will have in deciding which of them you will recognize as

having the floor. Who, among the greater Vancouver members, will be on his feet to take over where I leave off in an endeavour -and I hope the Vancouver papers will carry this-in an endeavour to put before the house the reasons why we should not allow an increase to the extent asked in the present bill? Who among them will ask for this limitation, and the granting only of sufficient money-perhaps $20 million by way of increase-to allow them to carry on? They claim this is necessary in order to produce the service required under the officials they have in Vancouver. This will be used to sustain-I was going to use a word I probably should npt use as it might be offensive to these gentlemen in Montreal-I was going to say this phony company, this fictitious company, but I will just say this unnecessary company, the parent they have in Montreal which receives $181,000 for $3,100 worth of experience and advice. That advice is so poorly thought of that the income tax people would not let them deduct it.

I know the hon. member desires to be fair. I ask him if it is not a fact that the decision of the income tax department in connection with that contract was made before the contract was ruled upon by a judicial body and decided to be legitimate.

If that is correct, I am glad to know it. I hope that this coming year the income tax people will reverse their decision and not permit the people of British Columbia to be milked for $181,000 for $3,100 worth of services. I am glad to have it on the record if that is a fact. That is just one more thing the board of transport commissioners should consider and render a decision upon.
I intended to move an amendment when the bill was in committee, but as I mentioned my seconder is not in the house. I have not had time to confer with the hon. member for Comox-Alberni or anyone else, but I move, seconded by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni:
That section 6, clause 1, of Bill E be amended by striking out all the words on the eleventh line after "exceed" and the following words added, "thirty-five million dollars."

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Out of order.

I believe I am allowed to say one word after having moved the amendment. I would assume that any decision as to the amendment being in order or out of order will be made by Your Honour rather than by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.
Is the house ready for the question?

I would draw to your attention that we are dealing with the motion for the second reading of the bill and in my submission an amendment to one of the sections is out of order and should not be placed before the house when it is considering the principle of the bill.

Mr. Speaker, while you are considering that question I think it might have some bearing if the house were to know whether the seconder of the amendment had had an opportunity to see it before he seconded it. From the sudden change indicated by the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank) it would seem quite certain that the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Gibson) has not seen the amendment which he seconded. Perhaps he would change his mind if he had an opportunity to see it.
I am delighted that the hon. member for Kamloops has seen fit to advise me in this matter, but I can assure you that I am quite pleased to second the amendment and I know all about It.

I had hoped that a number of hon. members would have expressed opinions as to whether this amendment is in order. Does any other hon. member desire to speak on the point of order? Without doubt the view expressed by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Applewhaite) is correct. When we are considering the principle of a bill it is not in order to move an amendment to one of the sections. Accordingly I shall have to rule the amendment out of order.

Mr. Speaker, I believe the house is in debt to the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Applewhaite) for the able way in which he has presented the motion for second reading and for the information he has given us while speaking in support of his motion. There are a number of questions-in saying this I do not take away from the sincerity of my first words- which I think we are entitled to ask in order that we may have further details before the motion for second reading is decided upon. I should like to deal with some of these tonight and to place certain considerations before the hon. member which we would appreciate having him deal with when he replies.
Then the hon. tnember for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank) raised a point in connection with the increase in capital which the company is asking for. As I see it, this bill divides itself conveniently into two objectives. The first is to obtain authority from this house to increase the share value by $50 million, from $25 million to $75 million. The
British Columbia Telephone Company second is to ask this house to amend the incorporating act to permit a reorganization of the capital structure, a subdivision of the common shares and also a subdivision of the preference shares, with certain other incidental consequences.
The hon. member for Fraser Valley has raised a point in connection with the first of these two objectives, that is, the increase in the capital which is requested. I think that point is one about which we should hear more from the hon. member for Skeena. As the hon. member for Fraser Valley has correctly pointed out, this increase of $50 million in the share capital would not only have the effect of allowing the company to increase its working capital by $50 million- I hope the hon. member for Skeena will correct me if I am wrong-but I understand the practice of the company is to finance its operation with approximately 50 per cent of share capital and 50 per cent of bonds.
If they obtain authority to issue and in fact do issue another $50 million of shares, as those shares were issued and in accordance with their normal practice they could float bond issues of approximately the same value. Possibly they might not issue all the $50 million of shares at once; they would perhaps issue $10 million and about the same time they would normally float a bond issue of the same value. According to their method of financing, if this $50 million increase is granted it would mean that this company could avail itself of $100 million additional working capital through the issue of shares and the floating of bonds.
The point has been raised by the hon. member for Fraser Valley that such a large increase in capital would enable the company to carry on for a great length of time without the necessity of coming back to this house. I think that point is well taken. It is of increasing seriousness in the light of the ordinary practice of this company with respect to financing. I am making no suggestion that that is an improper method of financing. I am merely drawing to the attention of the house that that is the normal practice followed by this company and I understand that they do not intend to depart from that practice. So I ask the house to have it in mind that this bill may have an over-all effect of giving this company another $100 million to go on with. I think the house should consider that in the light of the point raised by the hon. member for Fraser Valley with respect to the rate of increases, with respect to the fact that the only time when parliament at any rate has a chance to express its opinion concerning the operations of this company is when it comes before parliament for an
1344	HOUSE OF COMMONS
British Columbia Telephone Company increase in capital, and also in the light of the fact that the city of Vancouver has presented a very well reasoned and excellent brief questioning the propriety of granting this large amount of increase of $50 million.
I think there is no doubt that the company requires additional capital. The hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Applewhaite) has told us of some of the plans of the company. He has told us of the great backlog of applications for additional telephones which the company has on its files. The majority of members from British Columbia have had the opportunity of interviewing the solicitor who is acting for the company in connection with this bill. I should like to associate myself with what the hon. member for Fraser Valley said about him as to his qualifications and integrity. I am not so certain that I necessarily wish to see him get another fee because he comes back to parliament. I think from what I know of his business that he does not require it to be able to conduct a very successful and prominent business.
Members have had an opportunity to see him, and he has -made a very good case indeed for an increase in capital. I do not feel, however, without further consideration, that he has substantiated a case for an increase of $50 million at this time which would have the effect of giving them another $100 million working capital, and which would in turn have the effect that until that capital was exhausted they would not have to come back to parliament for a review of their operations. It might well be that in the eyes of the company that would not be a bad thing. I can imagine that they are not anxious to come before parliament. One hears the suggestion occasionally that these bills are held up. I am quite sure that this measure, whether amended or not, will be considered and dealt with at this session. I do not think it does the company any harm, and I think it is an opportunity which parliament should have to keep the bill before it for several days so that the matter may be thoroughly considered, because the interests of the province of British Columbia are certainly bound up in this question.
At the moment I do not propose to express myself definitely against the increase of $50 million. I wish to hear more from those members who have studied the brief of the city of Vancouver, and I wish to have the opportunity of hearing further from the hon. member for Skeena before finally deciding on that point. But there is another point, Mr. Speaker, which I think should be drawn to the attention of the house, and it has to do with the second object of the bill, to effect a re-organization of the capital structure of the

company. What I wish to refer to particularly here is that portion of the bill which deals with preference shares. This company was incorporated as the Western Canada Telephone Company by an act of the federal house in 1916. I should pause here to interject that prior to that time it had been a company operating under a provincial charter from the province of British Columbia.
In 1916 it was decided by the directors that the scope of their operations was expanding and they desired to make connections with other telephone companies. As a matter of fact there were financial affiliations which took it outside the sphere of the province. It was decided to apply for incorporation by an act of this house and the works were declared to be for the general advantage of Canada. By section 5 of the statute, being chapter 66 of the statutes of 1916, it was provided:
The company, If previously authorized by resolution passed by the ordinary shareholders at any annual meeting or at any special general meeting duly called for that purpose, at which meeting shareholders representing at least three-fourths in value of the subscribed ordinary stock of the company are present or represented by proxy, may issue any portion of its capital, whether part of the original stock or any increase thereof as preference stock, and preference stock so issued shall have such preference and priority as respects dividends, capital or otherwise over ordinary stock or such qualified rights as is declared by such resolution.
Under the authority then obtained, and subsequent authorities, there was in fact issued $5 million of preference stock divided as of $500,000 original preference shares and $4,500,000 preference shares. These shares bear a fixed cumulative dividend of six per cent which represents, as hon. members will appreciate, what might very properly be described as a gilt-edged security. I would draw your attention, Mr. Speaker, and the attention of the house particularly to the , terms of subsection 2 of section 5 of the incorporating act to which I have already referred, which reads as follows:
Holders of preference shares shall not have any right of voting at meetings of the company except the right to attend and vote at general meetings on any question directly affecting any of the rights or privileges attached to such shares, and then there shall be one vote per share, but no change in the rights or privileges shall be made unless the holders of seventy-five per cent of the preference shares agree to same, and such shares shall not qualify any person to be a director of the eompany.
These shares were issued with a value of $100, and each share entitles the holder to one vote per share. No change in the rights of the preference shareholders can be made without the consent of seventy-five per cent of such shareholders. Subsection 2 of section 5 of the act of 1916 was subsequently changed

by chapter 36 of the statutes of 1940-41. I might say at this point that in 1940 a former hon. member from Vancouver, the late Senator McGeer, and also at one time mayor of Vancouver for a considerable period, introduced a bill which had the effect of increasing the capital of the company and altering the structure with regard to preference shares. The effect of the alteration with regard to preference shares would have been to interfere seriously with their preferred position, and to provide that their rights might be taken away, in a manner of speaking, without their full consent.
That point was raised and was debated at some length in this house at that time. The result was that the sponsor of the bill, after consultation with the critics, introduced an amendment to his own bill which had a much less drastic effect on the rights of the preference shareholders. That is now incorporated as section 1 of chapter 36 of the statutes of 1940-41. It has the effect of amending subsection 2 of section 5 of the original act so that it now reads as follows:
Holders of preference shares shall not have any right of voting at meetings of the company except the right to attend and vote at general meetings on any question directly affecting any of the rights or privileges attached to such shares, and' then there shall be one vote per share, but no change in the rights or privileges shall be made unless the holders of seventy-five per centum of the preference shares agree to same, and ownership of ordinary or preference or preferred shares shall qualify any person to be a director of the company.
I think it is important to note that the only effect of the change in that portion of the act dealing with preference shares was to provide that the ownership of such shares qualified the holder to be a director of the company. So the bill introduced in 1941 in effect was abandoned with respect to that part affecting the rights of the preference shareholders, and the only change made was that the holding of preference shares would qualify a person to be a director. In the bill now before the house it is stated that the only change proposed to this section of the existing act dealing with preference shares consists of the addition of the words "in par value" and "issued and outstanding" in one portion of the act. Then a new portion is added, and in the explanatory note it is explained as follows:
Subsection four of section five is a new subsection and its purpose is to provide that future preference or preferred shares may be of a par value of either twenty-five dollars or one hundred dollars each.
The reason for the amendment is that shares of the lower par value, namely, twenty-five dollars, may be more easily and conveniently marketed.
So far I have no objection or criticism to offer; I think it is perfectly proper to provide
16,	1951	1345
British Columbia Telephone Company that in future shares may be issued, either common or preference, of the pax value of $25, because they are easier to market. But at this point I make the reservation that if those shares are to be issued and if it is to be provided, as it is, that the holding of one share shall confer one vote, then I think we must insert a safeguard at this point for the rights of the present holders of preference shares of $100 each, which also carry one vote. Otherwise we will have this position, that preference shares of the value of $25 may be issued each carrying one vote, so the holder of $100 worth of new preference shares will have four votes as against the one vote of the holder of an old preference share of $100.
My objection to this portion of the bill is that there is no safeguard for the rights of the old preference shareholders. The bill provides that the directors can subdivide the outstanding preference shares into shares of $25 each, subject always to the consent of at least 75 per cent in par value of the holders of each class of such preference or preferred shares proposed to be subdivided. The important point there is that the directors may do that, subject to the consent of the present preference shareholders, but there is nothing to compel the directors to do it, and nothing saying that until it is done the holders of the old preference shares shall have four votes.
So this situation might well arise. Let us say there are presently $5 million of preference shares outstanding. If the company is authorized to issue $50 million of new capital it might decide that $5 million of that capital should be in the form of preference shares, and that those will not be $100 shares but $25 shares. The result will be that you will have four times as many preference shareholders and four times as many votes, because each $25 share is going to carry one vote. So with the new $5 million in preference shares you will have four times as many votes as with the old; and there is nothing to provide that the holders of the old preference shares shall be entitled to four votes per share as soon as new preference shares of $25 are issued. So under the provisions of this bill as it now stands and as I read it, it is quite possible to issue new preference shares of no greater par value than the present outstanding preference shares and yet completely swamp the voting powers of the present holders of preference shares by four to one; and I have already pointed out that the six per cent cumulative dividend rate attached to these preference shares makes them a gilt-edged security.

I am not attributing any improper motives to this company, but I do want to make the position clear. If this or any company, let us say, desired to make some change in the guaranteed rights of the preference shareholders while preserving the appearance of impartiality by issuing new preference shares with one vote per share and providing that the old preference shares might be subdivided to give them the same voting privileges, yet wished to use that in order to take away the rights of the old preference shares, this would afford a very convenient way of doing it. Preference shares could be issued before the old ones were subdivided, before they were given any greater voting power, so that while the par value would be the same the new preference share would have four times the voting power. I do not know who are the preference shareholders. I do not care who they are. The point I want to lay before this house before I conclude is that under our system of corporate and private law, established rights can only be taken away with the consent of the persons who have those rights. I may point out that shares of this type are particularly attractive to small investors, people with small estates, widows who desire a safe investment with a reasonable return; and I do not think this house should permit anything of this sort to happen without writing into the bill a provision which would safeguard the rights of the present preference shareholders.
The hour for public and private bills having expired, the house will revert to the business under consideration at six o'clock.

Mr. Chairman, the statement by the Minister of Trade and Commerce just before the dinner recess certainly came as a surprise to me. I thought under this amendment the government had intended at the end of this crop year, for instance, to take over what remained of the low grades, to be able to close out this year's pool and make the


final payment some time this fall. According to his statement before recess, he indicated that it was simply to clean up tag ends of certain grades or certain types of grades that might be said to be dribs and drabs of separate grades or separate varieties of grades being handled, without making any general clean-up of the pool itself. I do not think that is what the farmer in western Canada expects out of this legislation. He would prefer to see the pool cleaned up each year. As the minister says, that involves a certain risk to the pool of the preceding year. But the government have the authority under the act to set the price at which they take it over.

Mr. Speaker, before the bill is read a third time I should like to read an editorial. There appears to be a good deal of misunderstanding between rural and city people across the
1350

Canadian Wheat Board Act country. I have before me the September issue of Country Life, which is published in Vernon, British Columbia, by Country Life Limited. In this issue there is some sound advice I should like to place on record, in the hope that all parties concerned will take cognizance of it. It states:
Tonic Needed Badly
When an important farm group meets in a Canadian city, the businessmen, if given the opportunity, do not hesitate to declare that they are fully aware of the interdependence of business and agriculture and of the common and closely related interests of town and country. But they and the ordinary city folk are so immersed in their own affairs that outside perhaps of a few minutes every year, they forget about the farm families except to complain, without thinking and without knowledge of the facts, about the cost of food. Actually the main and essential foods in Canada are the cheapest commodities that are bought by consumers.
It would be profitable all around if city residents took time out once in a while and studied their relations with the farming community. Having done this, their sense of justice could go to work and1 lay the foundations for a better understanding.
A few plain truths, while perhaps not always welcome nor palatable, still provide a tonic that is badly needed in these confused days. U.S. Secretary of Agriculture Charles F. Brannan told a conference of business leaders some of these truths, as applicable in the States and even more applicable in Canada.
For example, one-third of the products manufacturing industries in the United States would be crippled completely, if deprived of agriculture's raw materials.
One dollar in every four of the revenue of the nation's railways is derived from the transportation of agricultural products.
American farmers spend two billion dollars a year on automotive equipment, their operation and their upkeep to the advantage of the oil industry and the car, truck, tractor and farm automotive machinery manufacturers and distributors and their employees benefit accordingly.
Farm families of Canada are buyers of goods and services of every type and in normal life, their ability to buy, governs to a marked degree the presence or absence of prosperity in the cities and in the nation.
Farm folk, through their federation of agriculture, are striving to establish close and constructive relations with city folk but there have to be two parties to this understanding and the handicaps are tough and numerous. One such handicap is the long farm working season during which agriculturists have neither time nor energy to prosecute good-will movements. Another is the absence of common meeting grounds. A third is the ingrained lack of interest of urban Canadians.
One of the best sources of help would be the daily papers of the cities but there again, the pressure of local, provincial, national and international news and affairs crowds out agriculture.
It would be a healthy tonic for town and country if the editors could find time to pay a visit to the agricultural areas and get firsthand views and firsthand information. These editors are most knowledgeable observers and they could render a further service of incalculable value to their country.
In my constituency I believe we have co-operation between town and farm people, who have made an effort to understand each

other's problems. I am sorry that some of the newspapers right here in Ottawa have not seen fit to state the true picture, and in this way are creating mistrust and developing bad relationships.
Motion agreed to and bill read the third time and passed.

I have indicated that there was general desire on the part of the government to get opinions from both Indians and non-Indians with respect to this legislation, and we have gone to considerable trouble to do that. Before I proceed to discuss in some detail the matter before the house I might state that the Indians were most grateful that this conference had been arranged. It was the first of its kind and in many instances was the first occasion in which representative Indians from the west met representative Indians from the east. The fact that they disagreed among themselves only made the meeting more important. They exchanged views and they discovered what I shall mention later, that the Indian Act is all inclusive and has to cover Indians in all parts of Canada. They realized that that had to be borne in mind, particularly by those who saw something in the bill that might not be applicable to their particular band or district.
Perhaps I might make one general remark before I proceed to a consideration of the bill. The most important matter to the Indian is his treaty and his treaty rights. I have pointed out already to the house that not all Indians are treaty Indians; in fact, just over half are under treaty as the phrase is used. There are something like 69,000 Indians under treaty, with a few thousand less than that not under treaty.
These treaties are agreements which were negotiated by commissioners appointed for the purpose, particularly to obtain the surrender of the Indian interest in lands. There are twelve such treaties and they affect the lives and the property of Indians from roughly lake Simcoe in Ontario to the Rocky mountains. In that area, as I said, we have some 69,000 treaty Indians. The treaties all follow the same pattern, surrender of the Indian interest in land, payment for that surrender, and certain conditions. These treaties are not referred to in the bill except in some instances where it was deemed advisable to provide specifically that they would not be affected by that particular section. The house will understand, however, that these treaties do not provide in many cases for what it is alleged they do. Any member who served on the Indian affairs committee of 1946 to 1948 knows that there was a good deal of confusion in the minds of many witnesses before the committee as to what the treaties did in fact contain. We do not accept responsibility for that, although we are doing what we can to
1352

Indian Act
overcome the confusion. These treaties are in printed form and are available in all our offices in the area covered by particular treaty.
I should like now to mention the bill generally without offending the rule as to discussing sections. Bill 267, the bill of last year, was intended to be a revision of the Indian Act. It was the intention to provide the machinery for carrying out government policy with respect to Indians. It was not the policy itself, and this has led to some confusion about the bill. Many people have written expressing disappointment that matters that they thought were essential to the welfare of the Indian had not been included in the bill. I think I should give two examples at least. I received many letters from people saying: There is nothing whatever in the bill about old age pensions for Indians. Similarly there were many letters saying: You have not provided in the bill that, wherever possible, an Indian child should obtain the same standard of education that a non-Indian receives. The house will readily understand why those matters are not contained in the bill. Those are matters which are provided for in this house by votes in the estimates and not by legislation.
Then there were representations which indicated a lack of understanding about what the bill did contain, and I think I should give one example of that. We have a section in the bill which provides that the governor in council may exempt from the restrictive provisions in the bill any Indian or any band if it seems desirable to do so. This section was designed to relieve the Indian from what might appear to be restrictive provisions. Nevertheless we received protests with respect to this section indicating that the writers thought that the government would try to avoid its responsibility to the Indian, and that the section might be used to destroy treaties, as the phrase was used.
Similarly we had objections from the other side of the story, that the section was going to be used to give to the Indian powers and authority which he did not want, which in some cases he could not use, and these representations were made by Indians as well as by non-Indians. I do not remember who it was now but I recall one person saying something which I think is significant. He said that the Indian wanted to retain his present privileges but to have complete political freedom from the government. That is a definition of the problem which has to be solved in Indian affairs. The problem is to maintain the balance of administration of the Indian Act in such a way as to give selfdetermination and self-government as the

circumstances may warrant to all Indians in Canada, but that in the meantime we should have the legislative authority to afford any necessary protection and assistance.
Heretofore we have thought of enfranchisement as being the ultimate role of Indian policy, and let us say frankly that we rather expected that the Indian would want to become enfranchised in order to be like one of us. Nothing can be further from the truth, Mr. Speaker. The Indian has no desire to become as one of us, and all his representations have said:	I hope you are not going
to take away from me the right to be an Indian. Of course there is no such intention. Except in rare cases the Indian has every intention to retain his connection with his reserve and with his band, and while he wants some of the advantages of our society he wants them on such terms that he can retain his old connections.
I think, sir, that our policy should be to extend self-government to all the reserves as soon as possible. It might be argued that this would give to band councils on the reserves greater powers than are now held and exercised by municipal authorities in our form of government, but if that would be the result surely we can impose safeguards to see that a band council does not exercise authority greater than a municipal council unless it is in the interests of the band. I think perhaps we can discuss that better in the committee stage.
This brings up other misunderstandings about the bill. Many people have written saying that they do not understand the difference between enfranchisement and voting at dominion elections. In fact I think one hon. member in this house during the debate last year showed that there was some doubt in his mind as to the difference between the two. Enfranchisement is the act whereby an Indian is released from the band, obtains the funds that are due to him and a small gratuity from the government, and goes out into the world on his own in nearly all cases. It has nothing whatever to do with voting at dominion elections as provided for by an amendment to the Dominion Elections Act last year. He now has the facilities for making his wishes known in this house by influencing the choice of the member who comes here from his particular riding.
One of the drawbacks to enfranchisement in the past has been that he could not do that without cutting himself off from his own band and his associations with his relatives and friends. It seems to me then that by providing the vote as we did we have begun a policy which will retain in the

Indian's hands all the benefits that he now enjoys by reason of being an Indian as well as giving to him, as I have said, the opportunity of influencing legislation in this house for his benefit.
I think I can see the time is not far distant when the administration of Indian affairs will be much better because in this house we will have a critical approach to the problem not just once every decade but every year, by persons representing the Indians. However, the word "enfranchisement", confusing though it may be, is difficult to replace. We could not find a substitute, so we have used the word again; and the procedure for enfranchisement is much the same in this bill as it was under the act. I want to repeat, however, that voting at dominion elections as provided a year ago has nothing whatever to do with enfranchisement; that voting at dominion elections under that amendment does not take from the Indian any of his treaty rights, though enfranchisement does.
This brings me to the question of councillors. In the bill we have provided that the election of councillors and chiefs on the reserves shall be by secret ballot. We think this should be the case. We think the Indian councils should take hold of the affairs of their bands and discharge their responsibilities, and that this can be done best by having them in the first instance chosen by the free and secret ballot of their people. Some representations were made that the Indians had not yet attained that standard of education in procedure and management which would make it possible for those duties to be performed; and it was suggested, you will see by the record of proceedings, that the term of office should be long so the chiefs and councillors might learn the procedure and methods of handling the money of their bands and dealing with property. For the same reasons it was also suggested that the term of office should be very short, and that we should pass as many people as possible through the offices, giving instructions as they went along. I do not think that is necessary. I think the term of office stated in the bill will be satisfactory.
One matter really counts to the Indian on the reserve; that is his property rights. There is no pattern of tenure of land for the Indian on his reserve. On some reserves they occupy lands by mutual consent. On other reserves there is an allotment by the band council, and in some cases there has been a succession of ownership passing through several generations. We feel this is not a satisfactory method for the holding of property, and that there should be some security to the individual Indians. We also feel that where an
Indian Act
Indian has had land allotted to him and has put improvements upon it, he should not be penalized upon enfranchisement. In the act at the moment there is a provision that an enfranchised Indian may live on his land on a reserve, or he may have complete ownership which would extend to selling the land. This has raised some concern that Indians might become enfranchised for the purpose of selling their land, so that eventually the reserve might be held by 'non-Indians. That has not been our experience. Very few of the Indians seeking enfranchisement have asked for the privilege of holding their land; but at the same time it must be admitted that many Indians feel enfranchisement should be a bar to any future relationship on the reserve. Others feel that Indians should be entitled to the same security of land tenure that is assured to the rest of us. But most of them agree at least that enfranchisement should not work out to the disadvantage of the Indian who has put a great deal of work and spent money on his land.
In this bill we have provided that upon enfranchisement the Indian may hold his land for a period of ten years. He may live on the land, and at the end of the ten-year period may have absolute ownership of it. That is a restriction compared with the present act, the only restriction I am prepared to admit; but it is done in that way in order to assure the band that there will not be a sale of land immediately upon enfranchisement. Let me say at once that we do not propose to use this in every case, and assuredly we would not use it if it would lead to any form of breaking up of the reserves or, in fact, to anything detrimental to band life.
Now just a word about the criticism which was directed to Bill No. 267 with respect to ministerial discretion. This bill does continue ministerial discretion, but I assure the house that this discretion is very much limited as compared with the present act; and in committee I am sure we will be prepared to defend such discretion as has been retained. In particular the minister is obliged to retain authority over the expenditure of band funds, for the very simple reason that these moneys are in the consolidated revenue fund and there must be some authority for their payment. I would not want to mislead the house. The ministerial authority does extend to supervision of expenditure of band funds, but I want to assure the house that just as soon as a band demonstrates its ability to handle money it will be given an opportunity of doing so.
I have not attempted to discuss many of the objections that were raised to Bill No.

Indian Act
267, but I think I should mention one objection raised by the leader of the C.C.F. and the hon. member for Lethbridge. Both these hon. members mentioned a claims commission and expressed disappointment that it was not provided for in the bill. There is no need for a claims commission in the bill, as far as having one is concerned1; we can provide for that also by a vote in the estimates. But I suggest to the house that there is no need for a claims commission in any event. Such a commission was established in the United States, but it was mainly concerned with a revision of the prices paid for land which had been surrendered by the Indians, in the midwestern states. In almost every case, if you will read the proceedings of the claims commission, it was alleged that the original surrender had been obtained by duress, or for lack of real value, or reasons of that kind. I think it is a matter of pride, sir, that no band of Indians in Canada has asserted that any original surrender was made under duress, or for lack of value, or under conditions similar to that. Under the circumstances we do not think that a claims commission is necessary for that particular purpose. Nevertheless a perusal of the Indian affairs committee proceedings of a few years ago will show that almost every Indian witness was of the opinion that his treaty rights had been abrogated or restricted in one form or another; and in particular, those who had treaty rights dealing with hunting and fishing.
In the province of Ontario it was alleged that, by the Robinson-Huron treaty, certain provisions were made for the Indians to hunt and fish in, roughly, the area north of lake Simcoe but that, by reason of the operation of the provincial game and fish laws, his treaty rights have been restricted. In the western provinces the suggestion is made that, by reason of the transfer of the natural resources to the provinces, the provinces have obtained the right-and are exercising it-of restricting game hunting and fishing in certain treaty areas. This argument-that is, the argument with respect to the western treaties- overlooks the fact that all those treaties provided for the regulation of these pursuits. On the other hand, it can be said that, by reason of conservation methods which are encouraged by this department, in co-operation with the provincial governments, the Indian has enjoyed distinct advantages with protection by having greater opportunities for trap lines, fishing rights and the like. Certainly the income of the Indians, particularly those in the western provinces, has been much greater as a result of these conservation methods. But the basic problem, whether confederation in the eastern provinces and the transfer of

the natural resources in the western provinces has actually resulted in an impairment of the treaty rights, is uppermost in the minds of the Indian at all times. There have been court decisions, and those court decisions have upheld the right of the Indian to hunt and to fish, in some cases, in what appears to be contradiction of the provincial game laws. In view of this fact and because we know that the Indian is reasonable, and because the Indian has expressed a wish to carry on within the law, we think that we should continue the policy of co-operation with the provincial governments in an effort to obtain the maximum conservation of game and fish, together with the continuing exercise of these rights granted to the Indian.
There is one other treaty right that the Indian asks and that is in connection with the matter of taxation. All Indians under treaty allege that they are exempt from taxation by reason of their treaty. There has been no court decision which says so. On the contrary, there have been court decisions which say otherwise. The point I want to make is thgt provision for tax exemption is contained in the Indian Act. That exemption which now exists is being continued in the present bill.
That brings me to the question which was raised in the house last June, one of civil rights, if you wish to put it that way, the right of an Indian to engage in lawsuits. The Indian may sue another Indian or a non-Indian or the government in precisely the same manner as a non-Indian may. In the bill there is nothing that alters the right he now has to do this. From the Indian's standpoint the difficulty is that his money is held in a common fund and he himself has no money, or at least very little, wherewith to finance lawsuits to assert his rights. We recognize that as a difficulty, so we have provided in this bill for greater authority of the band councils to use money for the benefit of the band and this may extend to legal expenses which they might incur for the purpose of asserting their rights. But I want it clearly understood by the house- and I do not think it was clearly understood, judging from the debate which took place last summer-that there is no restriction on the Indian with regard to bringing an action against the government for any right he thinks he may have had, or against any other person.
I notice that the speech from the throne suggests that there will be legislation removing the necessity for a petition of right; and that will apply to the Indian as well as to the non-Indian. I want to assure the house, however, that I am not looking forward to

a flood of lawsuits against the government, but I am saying this because among some Indians I met there seemed to be an opinion that they could not sue for their rights. I hope that if they think they have rights, they will take action in our courts to establish them, because our courts are set up for that purpose. I should think that the Indian would be better satisfied and that there would be equal justice if he took that course rather than that we should appoint a claims commission specifically to deal with his claims.
I want to mention briefly one part of the Indian Act which is not carried forward in this bill. In the present act there is a provision that the houses of parliament, by an elaborate procedure which is set out therein, might remove an Indian band from the reserve it is on to a newly established reserve, if the one on which they are living is adjacent to a city or municipality of over 8,000 population. The Indian has always felt that this was a reproach to him, that it indicated that he was a second-class citizen and that we did not like his standard of life.
I am sure there was no such thought at any time. But on looking at the section-and not only because of the opposition to it-we came to the conclusion that it was discriminatory and should have no place in the legislation of Canada. Consequently we have removed that provision and the Indian now is not subject to removal at the will of parliament from his present reserve for the purposes outlined in that section. We did that because the Indian is just as good a citizen as you and I. He may not live as we do; but I have heard many people say that he lives a happier life than you and I do. Certainly he has shown a remarkable adaptability. He is now overcoming some of the diseases which it is alleged we brought to him. But, at any rate, as a race, he is coming back. May I also add that he is getting wealthy too. We have in the consolidated revenue fund over $20 million of his money, including approximately $540,000 of personal savings. In discussing this bill it should be remembered that the Indian has pulled his weight in the two world wars. He is part of our community, in the more populated areas where he is part of a lively community he takes part in the community life, and he is indispensable to us.
I think we should frankly admit that in the past there have been shortcomings in the administration of Indian affairs; and in doing that we can only reassure the Indian by saying here that we are going to eliminate the shortcomings in the future.
Indian Act
There may be some legal problems to settle yet. There are one or two major issues outstanding in that connection. I might mention, for example, the Indians of British Columbia. They assert that by the terms of union whereby British Columbia came into confederation they were assured certain things which they interpret to mean no taxation on personal property. Whether that claim is justified or not is a matter of considerable moment to the thirty odd thousand Indians of British Columbia and because it is something in the nature of a constitutional issue, and certainly is based on a document which can be produced in court, we feel justified in assisting the Indian to come to a determination of this particular matter. We are making arrangements to see that that is done, and that the claim of the Indian is given every consideration by the competent court concerned.
I wish therefore, sir, to present the bill to the house and to ask the house to recognize that the Indian has arrived at that point, in many instances, where he not only can but should have control of his own affairs. We shall continue to give him that control as he demonstrates his ability to exercise it.
It may well be that the provincial governments can be most useful in aiding us in this respect, and it is a matter of interest that the legislature of the province of British Columbia has appointed a special committee to consider Indian affairs in that province. We are quite certain that the committee and its work will be beneficial to the Indian, and undoubtedly will be helpful to us in handling Indian affairs in that province.
The Indian is our brother, Mr. Speaker. He has been a faithful friend in time of need. Let us act as if he is.

subtopic: AMENDMENT AND CONSOLIDATION
subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in moving second reading of Bill No. 79, respecting Indians, the minister has already gone over much of the history of the old bill, Bill No. 267, which was introduced last year by the government. At that time, as a matter of fact, on May 5 of last year, the statement was made by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) himself that, if there was any great dissension among the Indians over it, it would not be passed last year but would be held over for some time. As we all remember, Mr. Speaker, that was not just what happened. It was given first reading on June 7, and came up for second reading on June 21, just two weeks after it was given first reading in this house. As you, Mr. Speaker, can readily understand, and as all hon. members can understand, Indians are found all across this country, and it would be utterly impossible for them to receive

Indian Act
the bill, study it and get their recommendations or briefs in to this government in a matter of two weeks' time. Therefore the bill was withdrawn and is now brought back to us as Bill No. 79.
As I see it, Mr. Speaker, there is very little change in this bill from the old Bill No. 267. I will admit that there are some good changes. I only hope that the bill is as good as the minister would have us believe it is.
I realize that on second reading it is the principle of a bill that is discussed; therefore I shall not mention any particular clauses but I do want to go over some points that are of particular interest to me, and something that the minister has just said.
Treaty rights, as the minister said, are very important to the Indians. They feel that these treaty rights should mean something. They were treaties made with the crown, and they feel that this government should uphold their portion of the treaty.
As the minister said, the Indians have fought in two wars, and were our allies in affairs before that. The minister mentioned something about taxes. Contrary to the opinion of most people in the House of Commons, and many people outside the house, the Indians do pay practically all the taxes that the white man pays, with the exception of land taxes on their property on the reservation and on income earned on the reservation. He is not subject to those taxes, but he does pay all other taxes. He pays the gasoline tax; he pays excise taxes on any articles he buys, just the same as any other person does.
The minister also mentioned the fact that the Indian was now given the chance to vote. I will grant that, Mr. Speaker. But what does he have to give up for the opportunity to vote? It is not just as easy as it is imagined by many people. He has to sign a waiver of rights of exemption from income tax. That in itself makes the Indian suspicious. He does not understand just what he is signing in many instances, and he thinks he is signing something away that is a right of his, and he should not have to do it to get the vote. It seems by some strange quirk-and the minister mentioned it tonight also-that this government thinks the Indian should be made a citizen of this country. Probably the minister is doing some crystal gazing. He admitted tonight he was wrong, of course. Well, Mr. Speaker, the Indian was the first citizen of this country. He has a better right to citizenship than anybody else in this country. We stole their land from them, moved them on to reservations and told them that they were wards of the state. Now we come along with this bill 
and say to them: We took your freedom a few years ago; now we are going to take your home. That is the point that I am going to try to bring out. Under this bill that is the right of the governor in council. They get that right under the assisting legislation that is put forward in Bill No. 79.
I have always maintained that where there are Indians of equal ability they should be given the preference in any positions on reserves or in the administration' of the department. It is only recently that consideration has been given to this matter, and I am happy to say that in the case of the Six Nations reservation at Brantford all of the teachers on that reserve are now Indian teachers. I am sure the minister can tell us how many Indians there are in the administration of the department, and we shall all be glad to hear that later on in the discussion.
As the minister quoted tonight, the policy of the government seems to be-well, I should like to quote again a part of what the minister quoted, which is taken from page 3938 of Hansard of June 21, 1950:
Indeed, it may be said that ever since confederation the underlying purpose of Indian administration has been to prepare the Indians for full citizenship with the same rights and responsibilities as those enjoyed and accepted by other members of the community. This aim has not been lost sight of in the preparation of the bill.
The ultimate goal of our Indian policy is the integration of the Indians into the general life and economy of the country.
The minister said tonight that there is a great difference between integration and assimilation. I took the trouble to look these words up in the dictionary, and I found that the word assimilate means to make like, to compare, to absorb into the system; while the word integrate means to complete by the addition of parts, or the binding into a whole. As has been said, obviously that is not the desire of the Indians in this country-most definitely not. So far as I can see, there is so little difference between the two words that I do not think the Indians are going to be any happier with the word integration than they would have been with the word assimilation.	.
I do not think I could do better than to read what appears in the brief presented last September by the Six Nations Indians, on that particular point. This brief was presented in connection with the bill before the house last year, but it would have the same bearing at this time. They said:
As is common to every national group, our prime desire is to retain our racial identity. We have no desire to be assimilated into the country at large, and only by preserving our reserves can we attain this objective. We had earnestly hoped the new act would give us the protection guaranteed by our treaties, but we note with alarm the provisions

made (section 42) whereby we could be removed from our reserves, when the only security that we know Is tied up in our reservations lands. Our people feel that the proposed new Indian act is an element in the long-awaited for campaign to abolish our reservations and defraud our people of their lands. If the abolishing of our reservations is the present intention of the government, they are only confirming our people's long, deep-seated fears and suspicions. The government can only do this by breaking treaties, and that is by breaking faith with a people who have never broken a treaty with the government. Let the government keep faith with our people, and with themselves.
And then, further on:
The white man in this country tends to get very excited about any threat to individual freedom, but ignores too much any curtailment of the rights of a group to an existence in their own way of life. Section 113 makes provision for the compulsory exile of any Indian or band, who, in the opinion of the minister, shows any progress or ability. We are opposed to group or individual enfranchisement which would mean losing our identity as Indian groups, and our personal identification as an Indian. We must be guaranteed the right to retain the land which the white man calls reservations, and which our people call home.
That is the point I am trying to bring out.
The minister has said that it is not intended to do some of the things set out in the bill. As I said before, in the debate on second reading one is supposed only to discuss the principle. However I do wish to call attention to section 4(2) of the bill because it is my contention that under it the governor in council has power to do almost anything it wishes to any reserve or to any Indian on a reservation. I should appreciate it greatly if the minister could point out that in this I am mistaken.
I am sure we have faith that the minister would not do anything detrimental to the Indians. Nevertheless as I read that subsection and note the power it contains I am led to the conclusion that it is an absolute contradiction of the democratic principles of British justice. Through it the minister could remove Indians from reservations and cause new bands to be set up, for which special provision is made in section 17. Bands can also be amalgamated.
I contend that section 4(2) does not give justice to the Indians. It would not be considered justice for white people; why should it be so considered for the Indians of Canada? So long as the government insists upon retaining that section in the bill I cannot give it my support. It is a complete negation of the other good sections in the measure. By this one section all that is good in it can be destroyed. I would strongly urge that it be deleted by the government, and also that the special committee of the Senate and the House of Commons be reconvened so that this measure might be placed before it for further consideration.
Indian Act
I understand the minister has said that he would favour that procedure if it were desired.
I believe that when the minister realizes the power he has in section 4(2) he will consider favourably its withdrawal. Certainly I hope he will take that course.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like first of all to congratulate the minister upon the frank statement he made. It is a pleasure to hear a minister explain a measure as thoroughly as did the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Harris) this evening. I should not like him to think for one moment that I agree with everything he said-because I do not. The fact remains, however, that it was a frank statement, anyway.
I shall not speak at length at this time because I think more can be done, and we can do a better job, in the special committee. What I shall say now for a few moments will be general! As everyone knows, most Indians are wards of the government and have no vote. They have no representatives in parliament and must depend entirely upon the sympathy of government and departmental officials. Under those circumstances the Indians at times suffer great disadvantages when they attempt to air their grievances or have injustices corrected.
I understand from different sources that the Indians in eastern Canada are beginning to take their place in industry and agriculture. While serving on the Indian affairs committee I had the privilege and pleasure of seeing for myself conditions among the Indians. Indians on the prairies, especially in the northern parts, and in parts of my old constituency, still stick largely to their original habits of living by hunting, trapping and fishing. According to information I received, when I visited reservations on the Pacific coast, it would seem that there are many instances where the Indians fit into the white man's life, where they work as loggers and fishermen. However, from everywhere one hears reports of the desperate conditions of poverty and the ill health resulting from the conditions under which they live.
With the Indian population on the increase this bill becomes necessary. It is not possible or desirable to treat Indians perpetually as alien enemies in our midst. They must eventually be brought to the stage where they can mingle with whites on terms of equality. We owe a great debt to the Indian. We got this great country of ours from them and in return we pay $5 per year each to all treaty Indians. That seems little to give in exchange for a country.

Indian Act
They are confined to their reserves and the treatment handed out to them is not always satisfactory. When the government made the agreements with the Indians they promised them education and medical care, and assured living room as long as the sun shone, the grass grew and the rivers flowed. None of those promises have been carried out to the satisfaction of most Indians. Changes take place rapidly these days and since the Indian lives largely in the past, and in the present, since he is largely untrained, he gives little thought to tomorrow. The adjustments in his mode of living made necessary by present-day conditions are beyond the thoughts of most of these men of the bush. Having been wards of the government for years they have grown accustomed to the care and help given by the Indian affairs branch.
I invite you to consider some of their problems. The education of the Indian is a difficult problem but one that is not incapable of being solved if approached with intelligence and sympathy. There are two systems in operation today, the day school and the residential or boarding school. Various religious bodies have co-operated with the Indian branch in establishing residential schools which are carried on at a charge of so much per pupil. The day school on the reserve, more especially in the north, is conducted after the manner of our one-roomed schools. This type of school is faced with the difficulty of the parents of the Indian children being on travel most of the time and not placing any value on education. In order to earn a living the Indians must travel most of the time and as a consequence regular attendance at school is difficult. This does not give the teacher much chance, no matter how good he or she may be.
No doubt the residential school was created to overcome the difficulties experienced with the day school. The pupils live at the residential school during the school year. They are away from their parents who are on the reserve. The boys and girls who are selected to attend the residential or boarding school, those whose parents are willing to let them go, are checked by the doctors and only the healthiest are taken, those who are free from t.b. and other ailments. Children who are suffering from t.b. and who need more care than other children are generally left at home.
At the age of sixteen years these boys and girls are returned to their homes on the reserves. The boy who returns from a residential school cannot hunt, trap or fish, and the girl cannot keep house in an Indian home. All they have to show for their years at school is a superiority complex and a grouch.

The children who attend the day school on the reserve receive the same education as the children attending the residential school, but they have the opportunity to learn how to live on the reserve under existing conditions. The boys learn how to hunt, trap and fish and do other things essential to their future life in the bush. The girls learn to make bannock under primitive conditions, and learn how to cook over a bush fire.
The boys and girls who attend the residential school learn agriculture and domestic science in addition to the subjects taught at the day school.' They are well taken care of, have good food and clothing. But in the north country neither agriculture nor domestic science fits into the reserve picture of today. Children attending these schools have to learn to speak English while their parents may only speak the native tongue. The girls learn to wash and cook by electricity and they become accustomed to other modern living conditions of the white people. The boys see modern agricultural implements at work. In neither case do these children find an opportunity to use these things in the environment to which they go back.
No doubt the faults in this system could be corrected by taking the more promising pupils away for further education. The boys could be sent to vocational schools to learn trades and skills, while the girls could be trained as nurses. They would no doubt be able to return as -men and women to act as leaders in the community they had left when young. Those who have studied the Indians assure me that there are some who show great promise and aptitude to learn leadership and who would make good leaders in their communities.
Previously I have pointed out to the house how clever Indians are when in the bush. I have seen them there and it is really remarkable what they can do. I am quite hopeful that, if they are given the; opportunity, especially after what I have seen done in New Zealand with the Maoris, after twenty-five years we will see a tremendous difference in our Indians. The Indian will have to be fitted into our economy. While it may take years, the sooner we start, the better. It is to be hoped that the day is not far distant when every reserve will have its own day school. The best teachers should be encouraged to take up this work. They should be paid and treated so well that they will take on the teaching of Indians as a lifework of a missionary nature.
Outstanding Indian students should be permitted to work for a university degree and carry on studies that will train them for the

complex task of assisting their own people who today stand bewildered between two totally different cultures.
Coming to the economic needs of the Indian, little can be done in any direction until a more satisfactory economic basis is laid down for them. In the past the Indian was wholly dependent for his means of subsistence on the bush and the lake. Then the coming of traders provided employment for them, and in some cases a better market for their products. The old sources of food have gradually been disappearing.
The airplane is supplanting the canoe for passenger and freight traffic. One can make a journey into the wilderness today in comfort in an hour or two which would require days by canoe, to say nothing of mosquitoes, black flies, portages and hard beds on the ground. There again the Indian has lost another source of revenue. There are still plenty of fish in the lakes but if commercial fishing should be encouraged the Indians will have again lost a source of food supply. Distance from the market has kept these lakes from being profitable commercial enterprises but with the development of the airplane fishing in them may become profitable.
A great deal could be accomplished by the existing teachers, missionaries and doctors if a community centre were established on each reserve. If a hall were secured that was suitable for handicraft studies, health classes, adult classes in English, reading and writing, indoor sports, boy and girl scout movements, it would be a step in the right direction. Never having had such a thing as a community centre, the Indians have no conception of what an important part it would play in their future life. If the government could start something like that on one or two reserves where there are good leaders I am quite sure that the Indians could be got to co-operate.
The problem of the livelihood of the Indian is more complex and difficult, and what must be done depends in detail on the part of the country under consideration. However, one principle unites all requirements, namely, that while the Indian was free to roam at large he gained his living by wandering freely wherever food could be found. Now he is confined to a small area and must get his living therefrom. I wish to congratulate the federal and provincial governments on the policy they have adopted to handle furs for the Indians. The minister talked about that a few minutes ago. Their money is divided into twelve payments. I think the dominion government does that in cooperation with the provincial governments. It is going to be a great lesson to the Indians
Indian Act
to know that they will get their money by the month and will have something to spend every month in the year.
As I said before, it has been a failing of the Indian that he does not look forward to tomorrow. Under the policy adopted the families of the trappers for the first time have known the security of a regular monthly income which can still be supplemented as usual of course by casual labour or the sale of hay and wood. I see no reason why the plan should not work in other districts. It protects the Indians and enriches the country at the same time. It is to be hoped that the project will be manned and operated almost entirely by Indians who are showing a great liking for the work. Something can be done by way of gardens in the patches of soil among the rocks but the Indians are hunters and eaters of meat rather than vegetarians, and it is difficult to interest them in any form of agriculture.
In the same way I believe that forestry and lumbering operations can be developed and probably fisheries on the west coast. It will be a matter of guiding them in the principle of preserving the resources entrusted to them so that they may become independent and regain their place in Canadian life. The Indian is not lazy and he will work well and hard at the kind of work that is natural to him. Canada owes at least this much to these people, who are true Canadians.
I should like to see the minister set up an Indian affairs committee. I am sorry that members of the House of Commons were not able to be present at his interview with the eighteen Indians, I think the minister said, who came to see him to present their pleas. If they were the same kind of Indians that I have dealt with in the past, I wonder if they were just quite clear on what the minister had to say to them. But no doubt the minister will tell us more about that.
When the minister was speaking he talked about land being held by non-Indians. Perhaps he will explain that further to us the next time he speaks. If one Indian has the right to sell to another Indian he would not be allowed to sell to a non-Indian, or could he sell to a non-Indian and thereby in the course of time the Indian reserve would be whittled away so that it was no longer a reserve. I am glad that the clause to the effect that a reservation could be moved away from a town has been withdrawn from the bill. In the maritime provinces we had two or three instances where towns were quite anxious that these people be moved elsewhere.
The minister dealt with the matter of a claims commission. I have always advocated a claims commission and I still think that one

Indian Act
is necessary. However, if the minister has the assurance of the Indians that they have no further claims then there will be no need for a claims commission, but from what I know of the Indians in my own constituency and Indians I meet from time to time they still have claims. I do not think that we should go on raising another generation of Indians for the next twenty-five years allowing them to believe that they have claims if they have none. It is only by a claims commission that I think we can overcome that situation.
I have not touched on the matter of health because the government has made wonderful improvements in health in the last seven or eight years. I have had the pleasure of travelling through the north country and visiting some of the hospitals.
