speechtext:
Office of The Prime Minister Canada
Ottawa, February 6, 1951
Hon. Douglas Campbell, M.L.A.,
Premier of Manitoba,
Winnipeg, Manitoba.
My dear Premier:
I duly received your letter of January 31, enclosing a memorandum setting out the conclusions that the government of Manitoba has reached with respect to the financial proposals presented at the federal-provincial conference in December.
I should like to assure you that your representations will receive careful consideration by my colleagues and myself.
Yours sincerely,
Louis S. St. Laurent
Office of the Premier Province of Manitoba
Winnipeg, January 31, 1951
Right Hon. Louis S. St. Laurent, P.C., K.C.,
Prime Minister,
Ottawa, Ontario.
Dear Mr. Prime Minister:
It has taken the government of Manitoba some time to thoroughly review in cabinet council the various proposals made at the federal-provincial conference in Ottawa December 4 to 7, 1950. We have given these proposals careful scrutiny both from the standpoint of their immediate effect upon Manitoba and their long-term effect upon Canada as a whole. Our views of the two constitutional amendments dealing with old age pensions and retail sales tax have been forwarded in a letter to Hon. Stuart S. Garson, Minister of Justice. The comments and suggestions which we submit in the statement which accompanies this letter set out the conclusions we have reached with respect to the financial proposals.
Let me take this opportunity to express, on behalf of the government of Manitoba, our appreciation that the conference was held and that proposals of the importance of those which your government made were presented for discussion at that conference. We are of the firm view that the people of Manitoba, in common with Canadians generally, have benefited substantially from the financial agreements which are now in effect. We believe that the continuation of the principles which underlie those agreements and the new federal proposals is basic to effective and harmonious federal-provincial financial relations and to a healthy federal system in Canada. The requests for the elimination of what we think are certain undesirable features in your government's proposals are made for the purpose of reaching an agreement which will be of the greatest possible benefit to the people of Canada and which will establish a more generally acceptable basis for future agreements.
We trust that the suggestions we make herewith will be given early and careful consideration by your government.
Yours very truly,
Douglas Campbell

maintopic: STATEMENT OF THE MANITOBA GOVERNMENT ON THE FEDERAL FINANCIAL PROPOSALS TO THE FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE, DECEMBER 4-7, 1950

speechtext:
This statement is intended to outline the views of the Manitoba government on certain features of the financial proposals submitted by the federal government to the federal-provincial conference in Ottawa, December 4 to 7, 1950. The Manitoba government is pleased that an opportunity was afforded the various governments to discuss the nature of the new federal-provincial financial agreements to come into effect at the conclusion of the present agreements. We were heartened by the fact that the federal government proposed that the fundamentals of the present agreements should be continued and that its views were presented in such a spirit of good will and amity and that that same spirit prevailed throughout the conference. We welcome the assurance by the federal representatives that the proposals were intended only as a basis for discussion, that each province should feel free to accept or reject them as it saw fit, and that there would be no attempt to impose the views of the federal government upon the provinces.
At the same time, however, we cannot avoid feeling some disappointment that it was felt necessary to limit the scope of the conference, and that greater attention was not given to other important matters which are of joint concern to the provincial and federal governments. In his opening statement to the conference, the premier of Manitoba laid particular stress upon the need for joint measures looking to the development of our natural resources and looking to the maximum possible use of our resources, our capital equipment and our manpower. In the unfortunate international situation in which we now find ourselves, it seems to us that there is need for more emphasis upon this aspect of our joint federal-provincial arrangements, and that we should not let our concern with the tax rental agreements and with old age security obscure the fact that, in the most fundamental sense, our strength in international affairs, our ability to support social welfare programs, and the ability of our people to meet the heavy tax load placed upon them, will depend upon the total productive effort which is achieved.
However, it is not our purpose to elaborate upon this point in this statement, but rather to discuss some specific aspects of the federal proposals.
We are gratified that the sound fundamental character of the tax rental agreements is continued in your new proposals and that the payments offered to the provinces will be slightly larger under the new proposal than under the existing agreement. Your estimates submitted to the conference indicate that the payment to Manitoba in 1952-53, the first year to which the new agreements are to apply, will be roughly $670,000,

Appendix "A"
or approximately 85 cents per capita higher than if the present agreements were continued into that year.
We fully appreciate that under the new proposal the guaranteed minimum payment is substantially larger than under the present agreement. The guaranteed minimum will, however, assist the provinces only if there is a substantial decline in the level of Canadian prices or if the general level of business activity in Canada declines, with the result that the provincial revenues decline while costs of providing provincial services remain fixed or decline much more slowly than revenues. In view of this fact it seems to us that under present circumstances the major consideration should be the level of the actual payments rather than the level of the guaranteed minimum.
In our view the small increase in the actual payments to Manitoba under the new proposal will make it very difficult, if not impossible, for the province to undertake any extensive increase in provincial expenditures in many programs which we consider to be worthy of added assistance, both from the point of view of increasing the wealth and productivity of the nation and from the point of view of providing a greater measure of security and service to our people.
In his statement at the opening of the conference the premier of this province dealt briefly with a number of fields in which we feel there should be greater recognition of the responsibility of the nation as a whole in supporting the cost of services to those citizens who happen to be located in particular provinces or municipalities. He pointed out the nation-wide character of our modern business activity and suggested that it was important to have in Canada a mechanism by which income and corporation taxes collected from these nationwide enterprises can be made available to support the services provided by the provinces and the municipalities in the many regions where the activities of those enterprises are carried on. After discussing this point at some length, he offered the opinion that in line with this principle the federal treasury should assume a larger share of the cost of such items as old age pensions, unemployment assistance, education, assistance to unemployables and health services. In addition he expressed the view that federal financial assistance should be made available for projects looking tov/ards the maximum utilization and conservation of all the natural resources of the country. With the exception of the old age pension proposal which, if accepted by Manitoba, may well cost the province more than the present arrangement, the only manner in which the federal proposals in any way deal with the cost of the items just mentioned is the additional 85 cents per head of population which the province will receive as a result of the change in the tax rental formula. In our view this is quite inadequate and leaves the provinces and the municipalities under the necessity of paying the heavy cost of services in these fields out of revenue sources which are not sufficient to support them.
One of the problems which arises out of this situation is the way in which the provinces deal with the responsibilities and the financial resources of the municipalities within their territory. We in Manitoba, in common with the rest of the provinces of Canada, have endeavoured to give as much financial assistance as possible to the municipalities within our province. To some extent this assistance is provided by direct payments to the municipality, but in Manitoba the largest single item is the grant paid by the province to school boards. By paying a substantial part of the cost of education, these grants to school boards reduce the burden upon municipalities by reducing the amount which the school boards would otherwise
be forced to ask the municipality to levy as municipal taxes. The Manitoba government has been anxious to increase assistance to the municipalities, but if the only additional revenue available to us through the new tax rental agreements is to be the small amount which I have mentioned, it will be very difficult for us to add to the size of our grants to municipalities and, at the same time, continue to maintain a satisfactory standard of services in other fields of provincial responsibility without involving ourselves in serious financial difficulties leading ultimately to a level of provincial taxation which is, in our view, unsound. For this reason the government of Manitoba, the municipalities, the school boards and the people of the province in general, are all vitally concerned with the size of the payments under the tax rental agreements, and we are all disappointed that the federal government has not felt it possible to offer payments on a more adequate scale.
In addition to our disappointment that the size of the tax rental payments has not been increased to a larger extent, we would like to record some dissatisfaction with the new formula which has been introduced for calculating the relative sizes of the payments as between the different provinces. We refer to the tax potential formula which introduces a principle which if agreed to would be likely to be reflected in future agreements and which would inevitably lead towards a situation in which payments to the wealthier provinces would be larger per capita than to the less developed provinces. In the present proposals this tax potential formula is not of great significance, but if we recognize the fact that tax rental agreements of this general type will undoubtedly be a feature of federal-provincial relations for many years to come, and if we recognize the further fact that the principles accepted in one agreement will likely establish the starting point for the negotiation of future agreements, then it follows that the introduction of an unsound principle in the present proposals is of more significance than the relatively small effect which it has upon the immediate future.
In all systems based upon the federal principle, and, indeed, in all government systems in which a senior government operates within a territory in which there are a number of other governments responsible for smaller areas, some consideration must be given to the fact that in a great many cases government services are provided and government costs are incurred in jurisdictions different from those in which tax revenues are collected. In recent years and to an increasing extent this situation has been met by instituting arrangements under which taxes are collected by the central government from industries operating over the entire area, and are paid out to the local governments in accordance with some formula which takes into the account the fiscal needs of the local government. In other words the formula makes larger payments in those local government areas which are less able to support themselves out of locally collected taxes. This principle was reflected in the system of fiscal need grants which existed in Canada during the 1930's. It was explicitly stated and strongly supported by the Rowell-Sirois report. It formed the basic principle underlying the 1945 proposals of the federal government. It forms the basis of nearly all the systems of grants from the Canadian provinces to the municipalities within their borders. In every case the government operating over the larger area makes grants to the governments operating in the local areas in such a way that the grants are larger per capita to those local areas which are called upon to support heavy costs for education, welfare and the like, while containing within their borders none of the great centres in which incomes concentrate and from which tax revenues can be collected in large volume.

If we disregard the statutory subsidies which are paid because of arrangements entered into in the past which are now part of the established structure of Canadian government, the essential basis of the present agreements is that the federal government pays to each province as a guaranteed minimum, either $15 per capita or $12.75 per capita plus an amount equal to 50 per cent of the corporation and income tax collections in that province in 1941. That guaranteed minimum is then increased by the percentage increase in population in the province and by the percentage increase in gross national product per capita in Canada as a whole. In other words, except for the item of 50 per cent of the 1941 tax collections, the principle is that of uniform per capita grants. In the new proposal another factor is introduced, that of tax potential, under which grants would be larger per capita to those provinces with larger tax potential, that is, to those provinces which have the best opportunity to collect taxes on their own behalf and which, therefore, have less need for financial assistance.
The present agreements departed from the principle of fiscal need to the extent represented by 50 per cent of the 1941 tax collections. The new proposal departs to a much more important extent by explicitly recognizing tax potential and by recognizing it not as a fixed item b&sed upon the past but as an item which will presumably be recalculated at the time any new agreement is under negotiation and which will increase in importance if certain parts of the country develop more rapidly than others. If it should happen that all parts of the country develop uniformly, then the tax potential formula will be of no significance and there is no point in introducing this additional complication. If, on the other hand, the industrialized provinces continue to develop more rapidly than the less industrialized provinces, then the tax potential formula will assume increasing importance and will be positively contradictory to the principle of fiscal need.
We do not argufe that fiscal need should be the only criterion. We recognize that, in dealing with problems of the complexity of this one, a great variety of considerations must be dealt with. But we do say that the grants out of income and corporation taxes should be at least as high per capita to the less developed provinces as to the wealthier provinces, and that the principle of fiscal need should not be directly reversed by providing larger payments to those very provinces in which income tends to concentrate and which therefore have less need of assistance.
It may be that in order to secure the agreement of the more well-to-do provinces, the payments to them will have to reflect in some degree the tax revenue which they could themselves collect. If so, we have no objection to establishing a payment to them sufficient to cover the amount of taxes which they could collect from the tax potential which is available to them. But if that is done we think that the sound principle which underlies all these arrangements should continue to be followed, and that increases at least as large per capita should be made in the payments to the less wealthy provinces.
One other feature of the federal government proposals which is not satisfactory to us is the suggestion that, in the escalator clause for calculating the extent to which the payments to the provinces under the tax rental agreement will exceed the guaranteed minimum, the calculation for gross national product should exclude the item of indirect taxes.
Appendix "A"
The provision for an increase in the size of the payments in proportion to the increase in gross national product per capita serves two purposes in the present formula. In the first place it provides an adjustment for changes in price level resulting from the general inflation through which the world is passing. In the second place it reflects changes in the total productive output of the country. Our officials inform us. that in their opinion the gross national product formula is probably the most satisfactory and convenient measure that exists for those purposes, but that it is not possible to be precisely accurate in such adjustments and that therefore the present formula must always be looked upon as giving only a rough approximation of the real changes. For this reason they think it somewhat inappropriate that a small refinement such as the elimination of indirect taxes should be proposed in a calculation which in itself is subject to relatively wide variation in estimate as illustrated by the fact that the official publication in which the gross national product figures appear carries an item entitled "Residual Error of Estimate" which has in several years amounted to more than $200 million. They therefore feel that the proposal to eliminate the indirect tax item is an over-refinement of little statistical validity in the light of the nature of the figures involved.
In addition we see no valid argument in principle for removing the indirect tax item. In proposing that it should be removed Mr. Abbott expressed the view that to fail to exclude it would have the serious defect that any change in government policy regarding the general character of taxes would affect the amount of the payments to the provinces. There are, of course, a large number of other ways in which a change in government policy would affect the size of gross national product and therefore change the amount of the payments to the provinces. Mr. Abbott illustrated the problem with the suggestion that there might be a decrease in indirect taxation; but the much more significant consideration is what the position would be should there be an increase in sales tax, either by the federal government or by the provinces. Our estimate is that if the proposed change is made, every one per cent increase in the total revenue collected in Canada from indirect taxes would reduce the payment to Manitoba something between $25,000 and $30,000 per year less than the amount which would be payable to Manitoba if the gross national product figure continued to be used as in the present formula.
If indirect taxes are increased in that way, the cost of government services, both in the provinces and in the municipalities, will inevitably reflect those increases, partly through higher prices for goods purchased and partly through the reaction upon living costs and upon the level of salaries which must be paid. Furthermore, an increase of indirect taxes by the federal government, or the introduction of indirect taxes by several of the provinces, would inevitably be reflected in the cost of government in other provinces which were receiving no additional revenue from that source. Under those circumstances it seems to us proper that such higher indirect taxes should be reflected in the formula by which the payments to the provinces are calculated. For these reasons we think that the proposal to eliminate indirect taxes should not be carried out.
Appendix "B"

maintopic: A SUMMARY OF THE PROCEEDINGS OF A CONFERENCE WITH REPRESENTATIVE INDIANS HELD IN OTTAWA, FEBRUARY 28-MARCH 3, 1951

speechtext:
1.	On February 28, March 1, 2 and 3 of this year, a conference was held with representative Indians and officers of Indian associations from all of those regions of Canada where there is an Indian population, except the Northwest Territories. The minister attended all of these meetings in the capacity of chairman. The deputy minister and officials of the Indian affairs branch of the department were also present.
2.	The main purpose of this historic conference was to discuss the provisions of Bill 79 to revise the Indian Act and to give the representatives an opportunity to present their opinions. Every section of the bill was read in the conference and was explained. Opinions were expressed and recorded, and if, after discussion, suggestions for changes were made, these were noted.
3.	Upon conclusion of this phase of the work of the conference there was a general discussion about all matters of Indian affairs and administration of the Indian Act which proved most useful and, where appropriate, will be used as a guide for future action by the department.
4.	It was evident from the discussion that the problem of Indian affairs varied greatly from reserve to reserve. It was recognized that the Indians of the several provinces appeared to have differing rights and experiences, and that these differences accounted for the variety of viewpoints expressed towards particular sections of the bill. Nevertheless, the opinions of all present were stated not only for the purpose of presenting the local viewpoint, but also in an effort to find a common, advantageous ground so as to advance the welfare of the Indian people.
5.	One of the representatives stated that as far as he and his people were concerned, they did not wish to have any changes made to the present Indian Act since they found it to be satisfactory for their purposes.
6.	Subject to this statement, the conference noted that there was unanimous support for 103 sections of the bill. Opinion varied with respect to the remaining sections as will be explained in more detail later. However, the results of the discussions by those representatives favoring new legislation may be summarized as follows: of the 124 sections, 103 sections were unanimously supported; 118 sections were supported by the majority of those present; only 6 sections were opposed by a majority of the representatives and of these, 2 were unanimously opposed.
7.	All of the representatives present at the conference agreed that the Government of Canada should continue to extend self government to the Indian band councils consistent with their demonstrated ability to exercise increasing responsibility.
8.	The representatives at this conference were assured that all of their representations had been noted and would be drawn to the attention of the government and parliament during the later stages of the Indian bill. It was also indicated that full consideration would be given to the suggestions made for alterations to those sections of the bill which did not meet with the general approval of
the representatives. To this end, the representations which were made at the conference will now be outlined to the house.
9.	The first sections to be dealt with will be those which were opposed by all of the representatives present.
10.	With respect to section 86, all of the representatives were of the opinion that this section did not go far enough in providing tax exemption for Indians, and they were opposed to sub-section 2 because it relates to a waiver of exemption under the Dominion Elections Act. They recommended that voting privileges should not be conditional upon signing a waiver. It was also asserted that under Article 13 of the Terms of Union between Canada and the province of British Columbia the Indians of British Columbia were not liable to be so taxed. It was suggested that some consideration should be given to amending the Dominion Elections Act in order to do away with the waiver.
11.	All of the representatives were opposed to section 112 which is the section dealing with enfranchisement after enquiry and it was drawn to the attention of the conference that the opposition to this section had been recorded in a number of briefs submitted to the minister.
12.	Of these six sections opposed by a majority, four (93-96) dealt with the sale to Indians, and possession by them, of intoxicants.
13.	Regarding these sections, there were three views expressed,- (1) that the provisions dealing with intoxicants contained in the present act be continued; that is, complete prohibition; (2) that provincial liquor laws be made applicable to Indians;
(3) a compromise measure, such as is contemplated by section 95, which would allow the Indians to consume intoxicants in public places in accordance with the laws of the provinces, but which would not permit them to be in possession of package goods nor to take liquor on a reserve.
14. There was a wide range of opinion with respect to these sections. Many of the representatives favored provincial liquor laws, while others were strongly opposed to any change in the act. It was said that the present liquor provisions could not and should not be changed with respect to those Indians under Treaty 6 in Alberta and in other parts of the province not covered by this treaty. Some of the representatives stated that if the provincial laws could not be made applicable to the Indians, they would be prepared to accept the provisions made in Bill 79. It is apparent, therefore, that with so many different views expressed, the conference did not reach any general agreement on this subject.
15.	The following sections were opposed by one or more of the nineteen representatives but were approved by a majority of those representatives present. The number opposing any of these sections never exceeded six.
16.	It was suggested, with respect to section 11, that the present band lists be accepted as final as to those on those lists, and not subject to revision as provided in the bill (section 9) and that the deletion and addition of names should apply only with respect to those who may hereinafter be added to the band lists.

17.	It was also stated by one representative, with reference to sub-section (e) of this section, that it was unfortunate that an illegitimate child of an Indian woman should be entitled to band membership.
18.	Section 12 (1) (a) (iv) dealing with those persons not entitled to be registered was objected to also on the grounds that it would be possible for persons of predominantly Indian blood to be deprived of band membership through the operation of this provision.
19.	Section 19, dealing with surveys of sub-divisions of reserves, was considered to be very beneficial by some representatives because they felt that it was only through these surveys that an individual owner could definitely establish his claims to land on a reserve. Suggestions were made that in some areas these surveys should be expedited.
20.	However, two other representatives were opposed to this section on the basis that it might lead to allotment. It was indicated that there was no objection to external surveys of reserves but there was objection to surveys for sub-divisions. For instance, it was pointed out that the Indians in southern Alberta were not opposed to surveys of reserves, but that the Indians of central and northern Alberta definitely were, and that because of this opposition no surveys should be made without the consent of a band council.
21.	Similarly, opposition was expressed by two representatives to section 20 (2) dealing with the certificate of possession, the reasons being that the allotment system was not suitable in Alberta.
22.	Sub-section 4 of this section, dealing with temporary possession, was objected to by one representative on the basis that temporary possession led to a feeling of insecurity and that once land had been allotted to an Indian by the band council it should be a permanent allotment not subject to conditions to be imposed by the minister.
23.	Section 32 was approved by all except two of the representatives of the conference. There was opposition initially to the section by one representative who took the view that the Indians should stand on their own feet and gain a knowledge of business by experience. However, this representative withdrew his opposition when it was pointed out that this could be accomplished by the frequent use of sub-section 2, and he was given the assurance that this sub-section would be used when advisable. Another representative, on the other hand, stated very strongly that the Indians should be given the protection provided for in this section and was in opposition to the use of sub-section 2.
24.	Section 61 (2), dealing with the interest payable on Indian moneys held in the consolidated revenue fund, was the subject of considerable discussion. It was the general feeling of all of the representatives present that interest upon Indian moneys should be not less than 5 per cent and it was suggested that the phrase "of not less than 5 per cent" might be written into the sub-section.
23. With respect to section 64 (a) dealing with the expenditure of capital moneys with consent of the band council, two representatives were opposed to this section if it were possible for successive per capita distributions to be made. They were of the opinion that only the per capita amount set out in a surrender should be paid to the members of a band and that the remaining amount should remain as capital funds forever. Other representatives, however, favored subsequent capital distribution.
26.	Section 66 (2) providing for the expenditure of money without consent for the sick, disabled, etc., was generally approved but some representatives were of the opinion that the expenditure of band funds for this purpose was not proper but should be made from public moneys.
27.	Similarly, with respect to section 66 (3) (b) regarding the expenditure of band funds for the
Appendix "B"
prevention and control of diseases on reserves, one representative stated that band funds should not be used for this purpose on the grounds that the Department of National Healtli and Welfare were providing health services to Indians at the present time.
28.	The operation of farms by the department on Indian reserves provided for in section 70 met with approval except for one representative who was opposed to this section because it did not provide for the consent of the band council.
29.	The taxation of Indian dogs (section 72 (1) (d) ) was objected to by one representative because he considered that dogs were a necessity to many Indians.
30.	The composition of the band council as outlined in section 73 (2) was discussed at length, and several of the representatives objected to the minimum number of councillors (2) as being too small. The British Columbia representatives, for instance, pointed out that there were many bands in that area where the councillors may work away from the reserve, and therefore it would be difficult to obtain a quorum at a meeting under this section. It was suggested that the minimum of 2 might be raised to 4.
31.	Section 77 (1) dealing with the tenure of office of chiefs and councillors was also discussed at length and by a considerable number of the representatives. Several of the representatives favoured the 2 year term of office, but other representatives were of the opinion that a term of 2 years was too short a period for chiefs and councillors to gain sufficient experience for the most effective management of band affairs. These representatives thought that a period of from 3 to 5 years would be more suitable. It was also suggested by one representative that the election of chiefs and councillors might be staggered in order to obtain continuity of experienced councillors on the band council.
32.	The question of absentee councillors (section 77 (2) (b) (ii) ) was discussed at some length and it was felt that the provision that the office of the chief or councillor becomes vacant when a chief or councillor has been absent from council meetings for three consecutive months was not practical with respect to those bands who do not hold monthly meetings. It was felt that it would be better if the section were to read "three consecutive meetings" rather than "months". Consideration will be given to those special areas where band councils do not meet monthly.
33.	Section 91 (1), which prohibits departmental employees from trading with the Indians without a licence, was opposed on the basis that it might permit the minister to issue a licence to a departmental employee to trade for profit with an Indian. Although it was pointed out that there are certain civil service regulations which prohibit full-time civil servants in engaging in other business enterprises, it was suggested by the delegation that if it was intended that this section should apply only to part-time agents, then this should be written into the statute.
34.	Section 110 (2) which provides for the grant of land to enfranchised Indians, was discussed by representatives who were of the opinion that this provision might lead to loss of reserve lands, but as the matter rested with the council to make the allotment and because of the ten-year waiting period, the section was agreed to.
35.	Section 111 (2) which provides that a majority vote is required for an order of enfranchisement, was discussed and it was suggested by three representatives that the percentage of electors required to signify their approval should be raised from 50 per cent to 75 per cent. They considered that this was necessary in order to protect the minority.

Appendix "B"
36.	The following sections were discussed at length but were accepted in principle by all of the representatives after clarification:
37.	It was felt by some of the representatives that Indians should be represented in the administration as a means of recognition (section 3 (2)). The representatives were advised that the question of the appointment of an assistant commissioner of Indian status was one which would have to come under the civil service commission as to recruitment, and that the matter would be given further consideration.
38.	There was considerable discussion on sections 5-9 dealing with the registration of Indians and the methods in which these provisions would operate were explained in detail to the representatives. There was general agreement with the provision for appeal of decisions of the registrar regarding the addition to or deletion from band lists to a judge of a county court for final determination.
39.	Payments to persons ceasing to be band members as provided for in section 15 (1)	(a) were
explained at length, but one of the representatives was of the opinion that the crown had no legal right to pay one per capita share of capital and revenue moneys of a band to an Indian upon enfranchisement. It was suggested that a person born into the band had an inalienable interest in property held in common by the band and, therefore, should be entitled to take his share with him when enfranchised. It was also suggested, in connection with this section, that in some instances the Indian band councils had not been notified when Indians applied for enfranchisement. The representative was advised that in the future it would be the policy to advise the band council whenever an application for enfranchisement had been received.
40.	Clarification was requested with respect to section 16 (3). It was thought by one representative that a woman, on transfer from one band to another on the occasion of her marriage, should forthwith receive the full amount of any surplus capital coming to her. It was contended that the minister should not have the discretionary power as to the manner and times at which such a sum should be paid to her. However, it was pointed out that the various cases would be reviewed on their merits, and where it was thought that the woman required the full amount of the difference to set up housekeeping, for instance, then it would be given to her. In other cases where it was thought that the woman concerned might use the money unwisely then it would be in the interest of the Indian woman herself, if the money was paid out over a period of time instead of in one lump sum.
41.	Clarification was sought with respect to section 18 (2) and the representatives were assured that the general intention of this section was to provide authority for the acquisition of land for administrative purposes such as schools, hospitals, cemeteries, and other necessary facilities which would be in the interest of the Indians.
42.	It was suggested with respect to section 28 (2) which provides for the issuing of permits to occupy or use a reserve, that reserve property should not be used privately without the consent of the band council. It was pointed out, however, that permits could not be issued under this section for long periods. Provision is made in this section for temporary use of reserve lands for short periods limited to one year.
43.	Section 34, which is concerned with roads and bridges, was discussed at some length. The question as to the upkeep of roads within a reserve that were, to a large extent, used by the general public was raised. It was contended that, in as much as the Indians paid gasoline taxes, the Indian bands should get the same share of those taxes
as are paid to the municipalities by some of the provinces. It was pointed out that the disposition of the gasoline tax was wholly within the competence of the provincial government.
44.	Section 35 was the subject of a considerable amount of discussion. One representative expressed the fear that it would enable a corporation or a municipality to obtain a statutory authority to expropriate parts of an Indian reserve. Opposition, however, in this case was withdrawn by this representative when it was pointed out that the purpose of this provision was not the wholesale acquisition of land, but that it was intended to cover the use of lands for public utilities and other similar services. This section was accepted after an explanation had been given.
45.	Re section 37 there was an enquiry as to the meaning of the phrase at the beginning of the clause which reads "except where this act otherwise provides" but it was pointed out for purposes of clarification that this phrase refers to action under sections 35 and 110 (2).
46.	When section 39 was discussed it was pointed out by one representative that Indians in the past had surrendered parts of their reserve without knowing thoroughly what was contained in the surrender. It was stated that where an interpreter is used he should be put under oath to give a true account of the terms of surrender. The conference was informed that the departmental regulations or instructions would be examined and that provision would be made for placing such interpreters under oath as requested. It was agreed that there would be no objection to using a nonIndian interpreter, but that in all cases the best interpreter available should be obtained.
47.	With respect to section 46 which deals with wills, it was suggested that it should not be left to the Indian agent to decide whether the Indian was capable of making a will under sub-section (1) (b). The conference was informed that the Indian agent did not make this decision under such circumstances, but that evidence would be obtained from expert sources.
48.	It was agreed by many of the representatives that section 49, which is concerned with the distribution of property, and that those sections relating to wills and descent of property were very beneficial and were in accordance with the recommendations which have been made in this respect. There was some complaint about the length of time it sometimes took to dispose of estates. It was admitted that there were occasions on which there was some delay with respect to the disposition of estates but this was due to a shortage of qualified officers to handle these matters. The conference was informed that, if necessary, additional staff would be employed for this purpose.
49.	It was claimed by one of the representatives that in the past Indian agents had acted in a bureaucratic way in the matter of leasing uncultivated or unused lands (section 58). However, it was pointed out to the conference that this section provided that this could be done only with the consent of the band council. The disposition of sand and gravel from reserves without consent was also discussed. It was pointed out to the conference that this would be done only where there was undue difficulty or delay in obtaining the consent of the band council. This arises where the council members are absent in summer months. The conference was assured that, in any event, leases given under such circumstances would only be renewed with the consent of the band council.
50.	Section 65, dealing with the expenditure of capital, met with general approval. One of the representatives indicated that some difficulty had been experienced in obtaining land for an extension to a hospital. It was pointed out, however,

that action could be taken under section 18 to obtain the land for band purposes and compensation paid from capital moneys for such lands taken under this provision.
51.	The provision of loans to an Indian (section 69) was commended generally by those who commented on it. An enquiry was made as to why these loans could not be extended so that they might be used for building houses. It was pointed out to the conference that the main objective of this section was to provide for loans to Indians for revenue producing projects and that housing, unless it were for rental purposes, was not revenue producing.
52.	There was some objection by some representatives to Indian agents attending council meetings (section 79). However, many representatives thought that the Indian superintendent should be required to attend all council meetings and that he should not deputize anyone to sit in for him.
53.	Discussion of section 80 (powers of the band council) revealed that several of the representatives were concerned about the regulation of motor traffic through their reserve. These representatives were informed that the band council would be able to make by-laws regarding the regulation of traffic within the reserve under this section. On the general question of by-laws, it was explained to the conference that by-laws which did not conflict with regulations made by the minister or the governor in council would be effective. It was generally felt that the powers to be exercised by the band council had been considerably broadened by the bill. The question of licencing non-Indians to operate businesses on reserves was also raised when sub-section (n) of this section was discussed. It was suggested that by-laws regarding businesses could also be made to apply to Indians in a business on the reserve.
54.	With respect to section 82 dealing with money by-laws, some of the representatives were apprehensive that the governor in council might have some power to force Indians to pass money by-laws to tax Indians. The conference was assured that once this section had been applied to a band action under it was by the band council.
55.	The conference representatives asked for clarification of section 87, dealing with the application of provincial laws, and was informed that provincial laws would not apply if they contravened any treaty, and/or any act of parliament, for example the Indian Act.
Appendix "B"
56.	Regarding the appointment of a Justice of the Peace, under section 105, the conference was advised that Indian superintendents would not act as magistrates, except for special reasons, and in areas where ordinary court facilities were not readily available.
57.	The remainder of the sections were approved after explanation.
